metadata.title: How to Get Your First Commercial Cleaning Contract (Step-by-Step)
metadata.author: Janitorial Empire
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to land your first commercial cleaning contract but don’t know where to start?

In this video, Janitorial Empire walks you step-by-step through the process of finding, pricing, and winning your first commercial cleaning account.

You’ll learn how to:
• Choose the right commercial cleaning customers to target
• Build a qualified prospect list
• Find the actual decision-maker
• Perform a professional facility walkthrough
• Estimate labor hours and calculate your costs
• Price a cleaning contract for profit
• Submit a professional cleaning proposal
• Follow up without being pushy
• Turn your first contract into more commercial accounts

Whether you're starting a janitorial business or trying to grow an existing commercial cleaning company, the goal is simple: stop guessing and start building a repeatable system for winning profitable contracts.

Your first cleaning contract isn't the finish line. It's the first building block of your Janitorial Empire.

Subscribe to Janitorial Empire for upcoming videos on commercial cleaning leads, walkthroughs, labor calculations, contract pricing, proposals, and growing a profitable janitorial business.

#CommercialCleaning #JanitorialBusiness #CleaningBusiness

segments.text: Most commercial cleaning companies don't
lose big contracts because they're too
small of a company to go for that
contract. They lose them because they
look too risky to that big client. If
you've ever walked a large facility and
then thought they're going to end up
picking a bigger company anyway, well,
this video is for you to show you how to
compete for those big contracts because
big commercial cleaning clients actually
are not looking for the biggest
commercial cleaning services to take
care of them. They're looking for who is
going to be the safest choice. And so in
this video, you're going to get 10
things that any commercial cleaning
company can do to look trustworthy,
established, and ready to handle any
large commercial contract even before
you have a big office or a big team or a
huge client list. You can do these 10
things and win big. And real quick, if
you don't know who I am, my name is Matt
Perry, and I'm a seven-figure commercial
cleaning CEO. We started from scratch
and were able to build our company on
contracts of all kinds of sizes
including very large contracts that
brought us well into the seven figures.
And on average, the amount of hours that
we spent in building our company was
about 5 to 10 hours a week. And so we've
been very blessed to be here and now I
help you scale your commercial cleaning
company the way that I did. So if you
want to walk into bigger opportunities
with more confidence and control the
situation and get taken seriously, then
that's what you're going to get from
these things that you can do. And if you
skip over these and just gloss over
them, you may continue to hear, "Well,
we wanted another commercial cleaning
service. They seemed a little bit more
established." And you might continue to
struggle growing your commercial
cleaning company with smaller contracts.
But the reality is everybody had to get
their first big contract at some point
and then they continue to get more and
stack them up from there. So, that's
going to be what you're going to get
from this video. What can you do now to
win consistently those big contracts no
matter what size you're at. You first
need to recognize that it really doesn't
matter to a client about how many
employees you have because clients,
sorry to break it to you, don't care
about you, they care about themselves
and how you can take care of them. And
so what's really going on in your
client's head is they're asking
themselves, is this company easier or
harder to use? And what you ultimately
need to do in all of your processes,
communications, and systems is make your
company come across like it is the
easiest one for them to use by saving
them the most amount of time and having
the clearest communication and path
forward. Because as you heard me say it
in the intro, to them it's more about
risk. And if some company is going to be
harder to use, it means that that client
has to allocate more time or attention
or resources to manage that cleaning
service, whereas one that's easier to
use feels a little bit more hands-off,
more valuable, and it establishes trust
easier cuz they feel like they already
know what they're doing or that service
that service knows what they're doing.
So it's ultimately a risk reduction
perception, which is really what all
these points are going to be all about,
but your key mindset needs to be how can
I make sure that this client or prospect
I'm talking with feels like our company
is the easiest option. Number two, you
need to have professional
communication. Look, I I I can't tell
you how many times I've had someone
share with me a proposal that they also
received from someone else we were
bidding against, and not to talk
ourselves up, but it's easy to stand out
whenever someone has misspelled very
basic words in their email
communications or they've taken a long
time to get back with that prospect,
which doesn't feel make them feel like
they're being taken very seriously. And
those things are important, but one of
the keys to professional communication
is providing clarity in the form of next
steps. So let me tell you what I mean.
Let's take commercial cleaning company A
and commercial cleaning company B.
Commercial cleaning company A is going
to be our unprofessional example, and
they may not say anything after doing a
walk-through. They may have said, "Yeah,
we'll get you a quote." But then maybe
the client is waiting a few days for
that quote, and they send an email to
company A, which is a bad sign, by the
way. If they send you an email asking
for the quote, you you need to do
something to fix that. But they they
say, "Hey, when are we going to get our
quote?" And then company A may reply,
"We'll get you the quote soon."
Okay, that's very vague. I'm not sure
what to expect.
I had to reach out to you. It doesn't
seem very professional, right? Whereas
company B, either during the
walk-through, at the end of it, or
right after the appointment, they send
an email to the client or prospect
saying, "Had a great walk-through with
you. We observed some very specific
things we're going to apply to your
proposal. We're going to have that to
you by end of business day tomorrow."
Which company came across more
professional? The walk-through is so
important, but it's everything around it
and the professional communication with
it. And that's after the walk-through.
Your communication before the
walk-through and how you guide them down
the paths towards success that they
want, which is a clean building and
their expectations around that and how
they're going to get there, that's going
to set you apart professionally. Number
three, you must control the
walk-through. And by control, I mean
taking this example of giving next steps
and clarity and to going actually a
little bit further with that and taking
the client deeper into their pains and
frustrations. Don't just visit the
facility and be overwhelmed. It can be a
lot to look at, but you need to think
ahead of time about what are you going
to need to see? What are you going to
need to count? What's going to affect
you and your operation, and turn that
and reverse that into questions that you
need to ask the client. And it doesn't
need to be questions all about things
that will help you, because ultimately
you're there to help your client unpack
their pain. But you, of course, want to
get operational with some of your
questions and logistical, which means
how the job's going to be done, who
needs to be doing what where, so you
understand what the client is really
wanting. And exerting control in the
walk-through looks like this. It's
instead of just walking in to a bathroom
and taking a measurement of the space
and just leaving. Instead, you would
actually ask them after measuring it,
"Okay, what's been going on in here? How
frequently is this space done? Tell me
about the history of what's happened in
the past that's been frustrating to you
or your staff. What are your staff
currently saying about this space?" And
then, of course, you can follow any of
the rabbit trails and and pains and
unpack more from there. And then, you
can say, "Okay, we're good on this one.
Show me what's next." Or let's go over
here next. Do whatever you can to guide
that walk-through while still respecting
their authority and their knowledge. And
because they're in that that space a lot
more than you've been, right? They stay
there and they work full-time in there.
But you still need to have some sort of
expertise exhibited throughout that
walk-through. And the easiest way to do
that is to just ask questions and get
your client's story. And just to show
you how important this is, Gartner did a
study and found that 17%
of buyers, and buyers are typically a
role in large companies, a lot of
industrial and large office buildings
and property management, and they only
spent 17% of of their buying time, their
buying journey,
in person with the vendor. So, that's
not even just 17% of their time with
you. That's 17% of time with everybody
else combined that's going to be walking
that facility. And then the rest of
their time is going to be paperwork
communicating and all that professional
stuff, right? But just cuz it's a lesser
time, doesn't mean that it's less
important. It means that the power of
that experience in person is so vital
because just that little bit is going to
influence the rest. So, look like an
expert and control your walk-throughs.
Number four, you need to demonstrate
documentation. This is something we've
seen directly impact all of our quotes,
not just our big ones. But whenever you
are doing a walk-through or you're
presenting your proposal, be sure to
mention a specific process and maybe
even show them some sort of document
with a step-by-step part that your staff
does. And so, for example, let's say
you're bidding on a large facility that
has continually had staffing issues and
they want you to help solve that. Well,
what you can mention in there is that
maybe you have a specific hiring process
and you just name it never-ending
staffing process. It's really cheesy,
but you name it something and then you
can just do a really short explanation
of this is our standard operating
procedure or SOP for how we go through
this process and vet our people and make
sure that you are never short. You can
even mention during the walk-through or
through any of the emails that they can
look out for a client success packet
that has everything they need to get
their services set up simply and quickly
so that you can start taking care of
them. But, those are just some examples
and if you're able to show them anything
on how you actually operate internally,
that just helps because these are large
bureaucratic companies, they got to be
that way when they're that big, are
going to have documentation themselves.
They're going to respect that. And even
if they're looking for a larger company
and you're still a smaller company,
you're going to come across like a
larger company showing that you have
documentation. And really what it boils
down to with documentation is not just
that you come across like a large
company, but if they were looking for
that, you would come across like one.
But, it boils down to clarity reduces
risk and the fact that you thought
through processes and it looks like you
know what you're doing even if you just
write it for the first time while
bidding on it, which we did that when we
first launched our company. We won some
very large accounts by thinking, "Okay,
they had this specific problem. We're
just going to name some sort of
procedure, write it out for it and
create it right now." And that's exactly
what you can do by demonstrating
documentation and giving it to them.
Number five, on your proposal, you need
to list an objective. I can't tell you
how many proposals that I see that just
list a price and here's how many times
we're going to sweep and mop, right?
They're not hiring you just to sweep and
mop. They're hiring you for deeper
reasons. So, for example, with a medical
office I know that we quoted recently,
we put the objective in there, obviously
our scope and frequencies and price, but
at the very top we said, "This proposal,
the entire objective of it, is to free
up the administrator and give patients
nothing unclean to to see." And you
might be thinking, "Well, yeah, duh.
That's like the purpose of the vast
majority of cleaning proposals." And
yeah, it is. But if you spell it out as
that's what all this stuff below the
line is supporting, then it's going to
tie their understanding to that
objective and have them fixed on that's
what I want. They really don't want to
see all these details. They just want to
see that to make sure you know what
you're doing, but they want to be buying
a solution to pain and a solution that's
valuable to them. And I can tell you
this that large companies are so so
focused on budgets and where they can
save money and where they can cut some
things, right? And we won a very large
contract because our proposal's
objective and everything below it
demonstrated that we could reduce the
amount of work hours for their head
facility person who was a very high wage
person and needed to focus on other
things. So, we were saying essentially,
"Look, we are able to take that burden
off of his plate." And what they ended
up doing was increasing their budget to
bring us in because it still saved them
money because they could reduce so much
more costs somewhere else in their
company. So, list an objective in your
proposals. Number six is what I'm going
to call proof or presence. If you have
any existing commercial cleaning clients
right now, you must get reviews if
possible and put them on a sheet, put
them somewhere. Obviously, go on to
Google or somewhere else online, but put
them somewhere that you can hand them to
any prospects when you're doing
walk-throughs or presenting your
proposals. Now, if you haven't collected
reviews from your clients just yet, what
you can do is emphasize your presence.
Or, actually, I'm going to add another
one here, you can use story. So, let me
explain presence and story. Presence is
simply you as the owner are there and
you care. One of the best lines that
we've used to win large contracts,
especially when we were first starting
out, was this, "Look, to this other very
large or maybe very established
commercial cleaning company, you're a
drop in the bucket.
To me, you're everything. Your contract
personally impacts me and I'm the owner.
I'm the highest that it goes in our
company.
So, no one's going to care for you like
I will. And so, you turn what would be
viewed as possibly a weakness into a
strength and what was possibly that
large company or large commercial
cleaning company's strength into a
weakness for them. And that way, it
benefits your client and they're
thinking in terms of, "Okay, yeah, that
makes sense. I get more attention, more
presence from the owner, the highest
level in the company." And not only
that, if you can take it to another
level, that's why story is here. Story
is if you don't have all these these
proofs and testimonials or or case
studies and all that, you should
definitely share any sort of case study.
It doesn't have to be many, right? Just
one, of where maybe you came into an
account or a situation and you turned it
around. They were struggling with this
thing beforehand, then you came in, what
did you do and how were the results
after? And obviously, ideally, they're
still a client, how are their results
now? You can still, without any
testimonials, provide contacts, like any
references. They can talk to anybody.
They can talk to someone you did one
time work for or ideally any existing
clients and just make sure that you tie
it to the relevance of them and in their
specific facility. For example, whenever
we're asked to give references, we don't
just give them, "Here's three
references." We actually say, "Here's
this specific reference and here's why
this specific reference is relevant to
you. They either have a similar amount
of traffic or had a similar problem or
they're in your exact industry or
something and we call that out for each
of those references and make it relevant
to them so they're thinking, "Wow, okay,
even if I'm an industrial facility
calling a charter school, then that
charter school still has something in
common with me that my company solved."
So, leverage any form of proof that you
possibly can, whether it's actual proof,
reviews, right, or your presence or
stories that you can share. Number
seven, this one is a biggie, give a
clear staffing plan. And since you've
watched this far, I'm going to give you
a golden nugget with this, you can also
say workload plan. And these large
companies, they they appreciate the word
workload. Essentially just means how
you're going to divide up the work. What
is the staffing plan? Who's going to do
what and when and how are you going to
bring new people in? So, specifically
what this would look like is you need to
tell them what roles are going to be
involved in helping support the cleaning
of the facility beyond just the
cleaners, right? Are they going to have
any onsite account managers? Are there
anyone like area managers or service
coordinators or whatever specific
management
roles that you have in your company? How
are they going to be involved? How much
time? And then the actual cleaners,
which are you going to do zones? Are you
going to do teams? Are they going to be
broken out in the specific schedules
across the facilities? Are they going to
follow what's already been going on? But
you ultimately want to give them a clear
picture of what services in their
facility are going to look like. Now,
building one of those can be a lot.
That's why it is so valuable because

eight, a specific process you need to

videos.full_text: Most commercial cleaning companies don't lose big contracts because they're too small of a company to go for that contract. If you've ever walked a large facility and then thought they're going to end up picking a bigger company anyway, well, this video is for you to show you how to compete for those big contracts because big commercial cleaning clients actually are not looking for the biggest commercial cleaning services to take care of them. They're looking for who is going to be the safest choice. And so in this video, you're going to get 10 things that any commercial cleaning company can do to look trustworthy, established, and ready to handle any large commercial contract even before you have a big office or a big team or a huge client list. You can do these 10 things and win big. And real quick, if you don't know who I am, my name is Matt Perry, and I'm a seven-figure commercial cleaning CEO. We started from scratch and were able to build our company on contracts of all kinds of sizes including very large contracts that brought us well into the seven figures. And on average, the amount of hours that we spent in building our company was about 5 to 10 hours a week. And so we've been very blessed to be here and now I help you scale your commercial cleaning company the way that I did. So if you want to walk into bigger opportunities with more confidence and control the situation and get taken seriously, then that's what you're going to get from these things that you can do. And if you skip over these and just gloss over them, you may continue to hear, "Well, we wanted another commercial cleaning service. They seemed a little bit more established." And you might continue to struggle growing your commercial cleaning company with smaller contracts. But the reality is everybody had to get their first big contract at some point and then they continue to get more and stack them up from there. So, that's going to be what you're going to get from this video. What can you do now to win consistently those big contracts no matter what size you're at. You first need to recognize that it really doesn't matter to a client about how many employees you have because clients, sorry to break it to you, don't care about you, they care about themselves and how you can take care of them. And so what's really going on in your client's head is they're asking themselves, is this company easier or harder to use? And what you ultimately need to do in all of your processes, communications, and systems is make your company come across like it is the easiest one for them to use by saving them the most amount of time and having the clearest communication and path forward. Because as you heard me say it in the intro, to them it's more about risk. And if some company is going to be harder to use, it means that that client has to allocate more time or attention or resources to manage that cleaning service, whereas one that's easier to use feels a little bit more hands-off, more valuable, and it establishes trust easier cuz they feel like they already know what they're doing or that service that service knows what they're doing. So it's ultimately a risk reduction perception, which is really what all these points are going to be all about, but your key mindset needs to be how can I make sure that this client or prospect I'm talking with feels like our company is the easiest option. Number two, you need to have professional communication. Look, I I I can't tell you how many times I've had someone share with me a proposal that they also received from someone else we were bidding against, and not to talk ourselves up, but it's easy to stand out whenever someone has misspelled very basic words in their email communications or they've taken a long time to get back with that prospect, which doesn't feel make them feel like they're being taken very seriously. Whereas company B, either during the walk-through, at the end of it, or right after the appointment, they send an email to the client or prospect saying, "Had a great walk-through with you. Bidding on commercial cleaning jobs is a topic many professionals strive to master. A deeper understanding of the process, coupled with hands-on experience, is essential for growing your business and staying competitive in the industry.

Matt Stowe, Chief Operating Officer of OctoClean Franchising Systems, brings a wealth of expertise to the table. With over 20 years as a sales leader, Matt has honed his skills and strategies to achieve exceptional results.

metadata.title: How to Price Your First Commercial Cleaning Contract (Real Example)
metadata.author: Channel Zero Marketing
metadata.shortDescription:
Someone posted their first commercial cleaning contract in a Facebook group and asked what to charge. 49 comments later, the answers ranged from about $750 to over $3,000 a month. Same building. In this video I price it step by step, the way I'd bid it as a brand new owner cleaning it myself.


📘 Get my pricing and bidding guides: https://cleaningcoach.store/


You'll learn how to use a production rate for the general clean, count restroom fixtures, apply your market rate, set a minimum so small accounts still pay you, use 4.33 weeks instead of 4, and price every account so you can hire someone to clean it later.


CHAPTERS 0:00 A real "what should I charge?" post 0:39 49 comments, wildly different answers 1:03 The best answer: do your walkthrough 1:53 $750 to $3,000 a month for the same building 2:10 Why the answers swing so much 3:19 My assumption: brand new and cleaning it yourself 3:36 Square footage alone won't give you a price 4:06 Labor hours: general clean vs restrooms 4:38 Production rate for a small office 5:15 Pricing restrooms by fixture count 5:53 Tile vs carpet: why tile takes longer 6:37 The blended rate formula 7:52 88 minutes = 1.47 labor hours 8:21 Your market rate ($28 to $30 an hour) 9:39 $44 a visit? Why you need a minimum 10:10 Once a week minimum: $300 to $400 a month 11:02 Twice a week: $65 a visit 11:54 The hidden time: setup, breakdown, laundry 12:58 Monthly price: use 4.33 weeks, not 4 14:03 The back of the napkin formula 14:52 What a solo cleaner actually makes 15:44 Price it like you'll hire someone 17:04 So who was right? 19:36 Lost a bid? Call and ask why 21:33 Recap: price any office in 5 steps 22:51 Send me your building


RESOURCES Cleaning business guides: https://cleaningcoach.store/ Why square foot pricing fails: [paste Video 01 link] Daily tips on TikTok: https://www.tiktok.com/@thedigitalmarketingmba

I'm Scott Blair. I've spent over a decade coaching commercial cleaning owners on sales, bids, and P&Ls. The Cleaning Biz MBA is where I teach independent cleaning business owners how to price, sell, and run profitable accounts.

#commercialcleaning #janitorialbusiness #cleaningbusiness

metadata.title: How to Price Commercial Cleaning Jobs Without Losing Money
metadata.author: Clean Ops Guide
metadata.shortDescription:
Not sure how much to charge for commercial cleaning jobs?

In this episode of Clean Ops Guide, we break down how to price commercial cleaning contracts without underbidding, overlooking labor costs, or losing money.

You’ll learn:

* Why winning a cleaning contract doesn’t always mean making a profit
* Why square footage alone isn’t enough to determine pricing
* How production rates help estimate cleaning labor
* The difference between pricing an office and a medical facility
* Why overhead, labor costs, and profit margins matter

We’ll also compare two 10,000-square-foot buildings to demonstrate how the same square footage can require significantly different labor hours.

This lesson is based on my book, Commercial Cleaning Pricing & Bidding Guide.

📘 More commercial cleaning education and resources:
https://cleanopsguide.com

📥 Download the FREE Commercial Cleaning Startup Kit:
https://cleanopsguide.gumroad.com/l/rzunfn

Subscribe to Clean Ops Guide for practical lessons on commercial cleaning pricing, bidding, contracts, staffing, and operations.

Question: What’s your biggest challenge when pricing a commercial cleaning contract?

#CommercialCleaning #CleaningBusiness #JanitorialBusiness #CleanOpsGuide

If an employee earns $20 per an hour, that doesn't necessarily mean the employee costs >> [music] >> the business only $20 per an hour. You may also have payroll taxes, workers compensation, insurance, training, and other employment-related expenses. [music] Then, you have the operating costs of the business, things like transportation, equipment maintenance, software, administrative work, and marketing. And, of course, you need to account for profit. Because if your business only generates enough money to cover expenses, there's very little room for unexpected problems or future growth. So, your pricing should follow a logical order. First, understand the building and the scope. Second, estimate the labor hours. Third, calculate your actual labor and operating costs. >> [music] >> And finally, build in reasonable profit margin. That process gives you a much stronger foundation than [music] simply guessing what the client might be willing to pay. Here's what I want you to remember. You don't need [music] to be the cheapest cleaning company to build a successful business. And you don't need to win every contract. You need to understand your costs, evaluate opportunities carefully, >> [music] >> and make decisions that support the business you're trying to build. If your estimate shows that a building requires 5 hours of cleaning, don't pretend it only requires three just to make [music] your proposal more competitive. The work doesn't disappear because you lowered your price. Someone still has to complete it, and eventually, that difference shows up in rushed cleaning, employee frustration, declining quality, or owner working extra hours to keep the client satisfied. A good price should allow you to keep the promises you're making to your customers. That's what sustainable pricing is really about. So, before submitting your next commercial cleaning proposal, remember three things. [music] Don't price a building based on square footage alone. Estimate the labor honestly. And make sure your price accounts [music] for real cost and delivering the service, including overhead and profit. These are some of the principles I cover in my commercial cleaning pricing >> [music] >> and bidding guide. Chasing a going square-foot rate sets the wrong monthly price for office cleaning.

Most office cleaning bids start with hours per visit.

Cleaning frequency, like Monday through Friday, changes the monthly price.

Divide the monthly price by cleanable square footage to get a price per square foot.

– Calculate monthly price per cleanable square footage

🩸What are Bloodborne Pathogens, and why are BBP standards so important in healthcare? In this must-watch video for medical professionals and students, we break down what bloodborne pathogens are, how they spread, and the OSHA safety standards designed to protect healthcare workers from HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C.

Learn how to protect yourself from needlestick injuries, accidental exposure, and other risks by mastering BBP protocols, PPE use, and infection prevention strategies. Real data, practical examples, and essential safety tips make this the perfect resource for anyone working around blood or body fluids.

Free classroom material at our Teachers Pay Teachers store
https://www.teacherspayteachers.com/store/active-engagement-learning

✅ You’ll Learn:
• What qualifies as a bloodborne pathogen
• Which body fluids are considered risky
• How HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C affect healthcare workers
• Key safety practices from OSHA and CDC
• How vaccination and PPE reduce workplace infections

🎯 Perfect for:
• Medical assistants
• Phlebotomists
• Nursing students
• Healthcare workers in training
• OSHA compliance reviews

📊 Did you know?
• Over 800,000 needlestick injuries happen annually in the U.S.
• OSHA BBP standards dramatically reduced workplace hepatitis B cases
• Hepatitis C has no vaccine, so prevention is critical

👉 Stay informed. Stay safe. Subscribe for more healthcare training videos!

segments.text: [Music]
What is a bloodborne
pathogen? Let's talk about bloodborne
pathogens and their importance in the
medical office. Remember that pathogens
are tiny organisms like viruses or
bacteria that live in the blood and can
make you really sick if they get into
your body. You might hear about them
most often in healthcare settings, but
anyone can be exposed if they come into
contact with infected blood. The big
ones we focus on are HIV, hepatitis B,
and hepatitis C. Knowing how they spread
and how to protect yourself is a big
part of staying safe, especially if
you're working around blood or body
fluids. When we say bloodborne
pathogens, we're mainly talking about
germs found in blood. But it's not just
blood you need to watch out for. Other
body fluids can carry these pathogens
too. Think semen, vaginal fluids, and
fluids from around the brain. Spinal
cord, lungs, heart, and joints. Even
amniotic fluid during childirth can be
risky. Saliva, sweat, tears, urine, and
vomit usually don't carry bloodborne
pathogens unless you can actually see
blood in them. Bottom line, if there's a
chance blood is present, you treat it
like it could be infectious.
Bloodborne pathogens spread mainly when
these fluids come in contact with broken
skin like cuts or abrasions or mucous
membranes such as eyes, nose, mouth. The
most common ways this happens in
healthare are through needlestick
injuries, cuts from sharp objects or
accidental splashes to the face. That's
why using gloves, masks, and eye
protection and washing your hands after
any exposure is so important for staying
safe. Learning about bloodborne pathogen
or BBP standards isn't just a box to
check. It's about protecting yourself
and your co-workers from real risks. Did
you know that over half of nurses, about
52% report being exposed to blood or
body fluids at work at some point? And
globally, about three million healthare
workers each year experience accidental
exposures to bloodborne pathogens
leading to thousands of new infections,
including hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and
HIV. In the US alone, the CDC estimates
that up to 800,000 accidental
needlestick injuries happen annually,
with many going unreported.
BBP standards like those from OSHA or
other organizations outside of the
United States have made a big
difference. After these rules were put
in place, the rate of workplace
infections, especially hepatitis B,
dropped dramatically because of better
safety practices and vaccination
requirements. But the risk is still
there and most injuries can actually be
prevented by following the right
protocols and using safer devices.
That's why learning and sticking to BBP
standards is so important. It's one of
the best ways to keep yourself, your
team, and your patients safe. Let's take
a look at three common bloodborne
diseases that we are concerned about as
healthcare
providers. The EIV stands for human
immuno deficiency virus. It's a virus
that attacks the body's immune system
which keeps you healthy and fights off
infections. If someone gets HIV and
doesn't get treatment, it can lead to
AIDS or acquired immuno deficiency
syndrome which is the most serious
stage. The virus spreads through blood
and a few other fluids like semen,
vaginal fluid and breast milk.
Healthcare providers are at risk if they
come in contact with infected blood like
through needlesticks, cuts or splashes
to the eyes or mucous membranes. For
example, a needlestick injury has a
small but real risk of HIV transmission,
about 0.3% for an exposure to blood.
This means that for every 1,000
accidental needlesticks, one person
risks contracting HIV. You can't get HIV
from casual contact, like hugging or
sharing a drink. Thankfully, with modern
medicine, people living with HIV can
stay healthy for many years if they take
their meds. Globally, there were about
38 million people living with HIV in
2021, and the number of new infections
has been dropping steadily over the
years. Hepatitis B is a viral infection
that affects the liver. It's spread
through contact with infected blood or
other body fluids like semen and vaginal
fluids. Healthare workers are at a
higher risk of exposure, especially if
they deal with needles, syringes, or
have any cuts or abrasions that might
come into contact with infected blood.
If someone gets hepatitis B, it can lead
to chronic liver disease, cerosis, or
even liver cancer over time. The good
news is that the virus is preventable.
In fact, in 2019, the World Health
Organization reported that the global
prevalence of hepatitis B has dropped
significantly due to effective
vaccination programs. The vaccine
typically involves three doses over a
six-month period. And once you're fully
vaccinated, you're about 95% protected
against the virus. Healthare workers
face a significantly higher risk of
hepatitis B infection compared to the
general population. Mainly because of
their frequent exposure to blood and
body fluids. The risk of contracting
hepatitis B is about four times greater
for healthare personnel who are not
vaccinated than for those outside
healthcare settings.
Prevalence rates among healthcare
workers vary widely by region from as
low as 0.6% in Europe to over 8.7% in
Africa. Often linked to low vaccination
rates. Most infections among healthcare
workers occur in high-risisk hospital
areas such as emergency departments,
intensive care units, hemodialysis
units, laboratories, and blood banks
places where exposure to blood and sharp
instruments is common. Needlestick and
sharps injuries are the primary roots of
occupational hepatitis B transmission
with the risk of infection after a
needlestick from hepatitis B antigen
positive blood as high as
19%. Unsafe injection practices and
lapses in infection control such as
reusing needles or inadequate use of
protective equipment have also been
implicated in outbreaks in outpatient
clinics, dialysis centers, and long-term
care facilities. Hepatitis C is another
viral infection that targets the liver,
but unlike hepatitis B, there's no
vaccine for it. It spreads mainly
through bloodto blood contact. For
healthare workers, that means the
biggest risk comes from needlestick
injuries or coming into contact with
blood through open cuts or mucous
membranes. The tricky thing about
hepatitis C is that a lot of people
don't feel sick at first, so they might
not know they have it. Over time,
though, it can cause serious liver
damage. including cerosis and liver
cancer. The CDC estimates that around
2.4 million people in the United States
are living with hepatitis C. A study
that combined results from many research
papers found that healthcare workers are
about 1.6 times more likely to get
hepatitis C compared to people who don't
work in healthare. However, even though
healthare workers often come into
contact with blood and other body
fluids, the number of healthare workers
actually infected with hepatitis C is
very low, about
0.13%, which is similar to the infection
rate in the general
population. Since there's no vaccine,
prevention is all about using standard
precautions such as wearing gloves,
safely, handling sharps, and following
all protocols for cleaning and exposure.
In healthcare, staying alert and
following safety steps makes a huge
difference when it comes to avoiding
this one.
[Music]

This means that for every 1,000 accidental needlesticks, one person risks contracting HIV. You can't get HIV from casual contact, like hugging or sharing a drink. Thankfully, with modern medicine, people living with HIV can stay healthy for many years if they take their meds. Globally, there were about 38 million people living with HIV in 2021, and the number of new infections has been dropping steadily over the years. Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver. It's spread through contact with infected blood or other body fluids like semen and vaginal fluids. Healthare workers are at a higher risk of exposure, especially if they deal with needles, syringes, or have any cuts or abrasions that might come into contact with infected blood. If someone gets hepatitis B, it can lead to chronic liver disease, cerosis, or even liver cancer over time. The good news is that the virus is preventable. In fact, in 2019, the World Health Organization reported that the global prevalence of hepatitis B has dropped significantly due to effective vaccination programs. The vaccine typically involves three doses over a six-month period. And once you're fully vaccinated, you're about 95% protected against the virus. Healthare workers face a significantly higher risk of hepatitis B infection compared to the general population. Mainly because of their frequent exposure to blood and body fluids. The risk of contracting hepatitis B is about four times greater for healthare personnel who are not vaccinated than for those outside healthcare settings. Prevalence rates among healthcare workers vary widely by region from as low as 0.6% in Europe to over 8.7% in Africa. Often linked to low vaccination rates. Most infections among healthcare workers occur in high-risisk hospital areas such as emergency departments, intensive care units, hemodialysis units, laboratories, and blood banks places where exposure to blood and sharp instruments is common. Needlestick and sharps injuries are the primary roots of occupational hepatitis B transmission with the risk of infection after a needlestick from hepatitis B antigen positive blood as high as 19%. Unsafe injection practices and lapses in infection control such as reusing needles or inadequate use of protective equipment have also been implicated in outbreaks in outpatient clinics, dialysis centers, and long-term care facilities. Hepatitis C is another viral infection that targets the liver, but unlike hepatitis B, there's no vaccine for it. It spreads mainly through bloodto blood contact. For healthare workers, that means the biggest risk comes from needlestick injuries or coming into contact with blood through open cuts or mucous membranes. The tricky thing about hepatitis C is that a lot of people don't feel sick at first, so they might not know they have it. Over time, though, it can cause serious liver damage. including cerosis and liver cancer. The CDC estimates that around 2.4 million people in the United States are living with hepatitis C. A study that combined results from many research papers found that healthcare workers are about 1.6 times more likely to get hepatitis C compared to people who don't work in healthare. However, even though healthare workers often come into contact with blood and other body fluids, the number of healthare workers actually infected with hepatitis C is very low, about 0.13%, which is similar to the infection rate in the general population. Since there's no vaccine, prevention is all about using standard precautions such as wearing gloves, safely, handling sharps, and following all protocols for cleaning and exposure. In healthcare, staying alert and following safety steps makes a huge difference when it comes to avoiding this one. [Music]

segments.text: The information in this video is based on the most current information available
at the time of production.
While Affordable Safety Training works hard to make sure these materials are current, the
employer has sole responsibility for compliance with all laws regulations and standards.
This video is sold with the understanding that AST is not providing professional or legal advice.
Employers should have a reliable source for current regulatory information and best practices.
Bloodborne Pathogens are pathogenic microorganisms that are present in
human blood and can cause disease in humans.
These pathogens include, but are not limited to,
the Hepatitis B Virus, HBV, and the Human Immunodeficiency Virus, HIV.
Blood-Borne Pathogens are transmitted in human blood
and other fluids that may contain blood.
This may include semen, vaginal fluid, vomit, feces, and other bodily fluids.
OSHA considers these to be potentially infectious materials,
which should be treated the same as blood.
Blood-Borne Pathogens are spread when blood
or potentially infectious materials contact a
worker's mouth, nose, eyes, or broken skin.
Needle sticks are the most common source of exposure.
Cuts from contaminated sharps such as broken glass
are another frequent source of exposure.
The Human Immunodeficiency Virus, HIV, is the virus that causes AIDS.
It is spread through blood to blood and sexual contact.
HIV weakens the immune system
and makes a person highly susceptible to illness.
There is no cure for AIDS.
Hepatitis B is a virus that attacks the liver it can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer.
It is mostly transmitted by sharing needles
or having sex with an infected person.
Symptoms include fatigue, abdominal pain, loss of appetite,
yellowing of skin, and vomiting.
OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires employers to:
Establish an Exposure Control Plan. Require the use of universal precautions.
Identify and use Engineering and Work Practice Controls. Provide appropriate PPE.
Make Hepatitis B vaccinations available.
Use signs and labels to communicate hazards.
Provide information and training to employees.
Maintain medical and training records.
Provide medical evaluations for exposure incidents.
Employees who have occupational exposure to
bloodborne pathogens must be protected.
Occupational exposure is defined by OSHA as
reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane,
or parenteral contact with blood, or other potentially infectious
materials that may result from the performance of an employee's duties.
Medical, dental and janitorial professions
often have blood-borne pathogen exposure.
First responders, food preparation, and child care
also frequently include blood-borne pathogen hazards.
Determining if you have occupational exposure is simple.
If your job task includes blood or other potentially infectious materials,
and you can be exposed to them,
you have occupational bloodborne pathogen exposure.
The employer must perform an analysis to determine job
classifications where all employees have exposure.
Classifications where some employees have exposure
and a list of all tasks and procedures that include occupational exposure.
Blood-borne Pathogens Prevention and Control Measures.
There is no way to determine if someone has an infectious bloodborne disease.
Workers must assume that all blood and OPIM is infectious.
This is known as Universal Precautions.
Universal Precautions are followed in medical facilities
and must be used anywhere occupational blood-borne pathogen hazards exist.
If you encounter blood or other potentially infectious material
assume it is hazardous and use appropriate protective methods.
Hepatitis B is a commonly transmitted blood-borne pathogen fortunately, there
is a vaccine available that can minimize the risk of contracting this disease.
Employers with occupational Blood-borne Pathogen exposure
must make this available to employees at no cost.
It is not required,
but it is one of the safest and most effective prevention methods available.
Engineering Controls are devices or equipment
that isolate or eliminate the bloodborne pathogens hazard from the workplace.
There are many common types of engineering controls.
Sharps disposal containers provide a safe method for disposing of contaminated sharps.
These objects such as needles, razors, or broken glass
must be disposed of in one of these designated containers.
Self-sheathing needles allow workers to cap needles
without exposing themselves to the risk of a needle stick
Engineering Controls are the preferred method
for dealing with blood-borne pathogen hazards.
The employer is required to regularly evaluate the
availability of engineering controls and
implement new controls as they become available.
Work Practice Controls reduce the likelihood of
exposure by altering the way a task is performed
The most common Work Practice Control is frequent hand washing.
Regular cleaning and decontamination of the work area is another Work Practice Control.
The employer can also prohibit unsafe practices
such as eating or drinking in a contaminated area.
Smoking or touching potentially contaminated sharps.
Personal protective equipment provides a
barrier between the employee and potential infection.
PPE is a common method of protection.
However, the employer has the responsibility
to try and eliminate the hazard with engineering controls.
If the hazard cannot be eliminated then PPE can be required.
Common PPE include gloves, face shields,
masks, safety goggles, and protective clothing.
The employer will provide work area specific
training on the selection and use of Personal Protective Equipment.
The workplace must be maintained in a clean and sanitary condition.
The employer shall implement an appropriate written
schedule for cleaning and decontamination
based upon the location within the facility type of
surface to be cleaned, type of soil present, and tasks
or procedures being performed in the area.
Contaminated work surfaces shall be decontaminated with an appropriate
disinfectant after completion of procedures,
immediately or as soon as feasible when surfaces are overtly contaminated,
or after any spill of blood or other potentially infectious materials,
and at the end of the work shift.
Disinfectants must be EPA approved.
OSHA allows for a disinfecting solution of one part bleach to 10 parts water.
Warning labels must be placed on containers of regulated waste,
refrigerators, and freezers containing blood or other potentially infectious
material, and other containers used to store, transport, or ship
blood or other potentially infectious materials.
These labels must be fluorescent orange or
orange and red and include the biohazard text and graphic
Red bags or red containers may be substituted for labels.
A bloodborne pathogen exposure incident occurs when blood
or other potentially infectious material contacts your eyes,
mouth, mucous membranes, or open skin.
A sharps injury is an incident involving a puncture
with a potentially contaminated object and is especially hazardous.
For skin contact, wash the area thoroughly with soap and water.
Flush splashes to the nose or mouth with water.
For eye contact, flush with clean water or a flushing solution.
If you have blood or OPIM on your clothing, remove it carefully.
Dispose of the contaminated clothing in a designated biohazard waste receptacle.
Exposure incidents must be reported to a supervisor for documentation.
Your company will make a free confidential medical evaluation available.
It will include a blood test.
The company will attempt to locate
and get a blood sample from the contamination source.
If you have not already received a Hepatitis B vaccination,
it will be made available to you.
If you observe an injury assume that all blood and OPIM is infectious.
Notify someone who is trained and equipped to respond properly.
If you are trained to provide first aid or perform cleanup,
follow established safe work practices.
Use Personal Protective Equipment.
Follow the company cleanup and disposal procedures.
Employers with occupational bloodborne pathogens exposure hazards,
must have a written exposure control plan.
This plan contains: A list of jobs and tasks that have occupational exposure,
Engineering controls, safe work practices, required personal protective equipment ,
housekeeping methods, waste disposal,
administrative and documentation requirements,
and much more.
The employer must inform employees how they can receive a copy of this plan
and include an explanation of its content
as part of the bloodborne pathogens training.
Bloodborne Pathogens are infectious diseases
spread in blood and other bodily fluids.
Universal Precautions assume that all blood and bodily fluids are infected.
Vaccinations are a safe and effective method for preventing bloodborne illness.
Engineering Controls eliminate exposure risks
and are the preferred protection method.
Work Practice Controls reduce exposure risk
by changing the work task. Washing hands frequently
as an important work practice control.
The workplace must be cleaned and disinfected regularly.
PPE is required when engineering controls cannot eliminate the hazard.
Watch for the signs, labels, and colors that warn you of a bloodborne pathogen hazards.
Use designated waste disposal containers.
Report bloodborne pathogen exposure incidents to your supervisor.
Know and understand the employer's bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan.

metadata.author: That Clinical Instructor
metadata.shortDescription: Bloodborne Pathogens training for healthcare professionals.

segments.text: [music]
[music]
[music]
They're too small to see with a naked
eye, [music] but they pose health risks
that are too big to ignore.
Bloodborne [music] pathogens. They are
the disease-causing microorganisms found
in human blood as well as human blood
components and products.
Exposure to bloodborne diseases is a
serious concern in the healthcare
industry. [music] And as a result, the
Occupational Safety and Health
Administration, OSHA, has developed
regulations for [music] dealing with
bloodborne pathogens in the workplace.
While there are a number of bloodborne
pathogens, [music] hepatitis B,
hepatitis C, and the human immuno
deficiency virus or HIV currently
[music] pose the greatest threats.
This program will show how exposure to
bloodborne pathogens can occur in
healthcare facilities, how regulations
and required procedures help to prevent
such exposure, and what to do if
exposure occurs.
[music]
The dangers associated with the HIV
pathogen have received a great deal of
public attention. It is reported to have
infected over 1 million people in the US
alone [music]
and it continues to spread. Symptoms
experienced at the onset of HIV
infection [music] can vary. They include
weakness, fever, sore throat, [music]
nausea, headaches, diarrhea, and other
[music] flu-l like symptoms.
But many people with the HIV virus show
no apparent [music] symptoms for years
after their initial infection. There is
still no proven vaccine [music] that can
prevent HIV and no known cure.
However, [music] great strides have been
made in treating HIV and there are
several drugs and drug combinations that
appear to be effective in controlling
the disease and relieving its symptoms
in many people.
People who contract HIV risk developing
acquired immuno deficiency syndrome AIDS
[music] which attacks the immune system.
This reduces the body's ability to fight
off other diseases and as a result can
ultimately be fatal. So controlling the
HIV pathogen is very important.
Hepatitis is a liver disease. It usually
results in an inflammation of the liver
[music] and frequently progresses to
more serious conditions including
cerosis and cancer.
Each year in the US, [music] there are
over 40,000 new cases of hepatitis B,
the most common type of viral hepatitis.
And it is estimated that more [music]
than three million people in the US are
carrying the hepatitis C virus. In fact,
[music] the prevalence of hepatitis is
so widespread that many experts consider
it to be a greater transmission hazard
than HIV.
While there is no known cure for
hepatitis B, a vaccine is available that
can prevent infection.
In some cases, the same vaccine can be
effective in preventing infection after
exposure as well. Currently, there are
also treatments that can help to control
hepatitis B and relieve its symptoms. In
recent years, there has been even more
progress made in the treatment of
hepatitis C. Today, there are drugs that
can actually cure hepatitis C in many
people.
Hepatitis B symptoms can take 6 [music]
weeks to 6 months to develop. symptoms
of hepatitis C from four weeks to 3
months.
The initial indications resemble those
of a mild flu. There is a sense of
fatigue, nausea, loss of appetite, and
possible stomach pain. Often jaundice, a
distinct yellowing of the skin will
eventually develop, as well as a
darkening of the urine.
In healthcare environments, bloodborne
pathogens are most often transmitted
parentally. [music] This is when
microorganisms that are present in a
substance are accidentally injected into
a worker [music] by a contaminated sharp
object. These exposures most often occur
through punctures from infected needles
[music] or human bites and are so common
that preventing parental [music]
exposures is one of the major focuses of
the OSHA bloodborne pathogens
regulation.
Other ways of transmitting bloodborne
pathogens include skin abrasions [music]
or cuts that come into contact with
potentially infectious materials such as
blood, human tissue, vaginal secretions
from discarded hygiene products, and
other [music] body substances with blood
in them. Cultures and body substances
[music] visibly contaminated with blood
must also be considered potentially
infectious, as must any body fluids and
materials of unknown origin.
Materials taken from infected lab
substances may carry bloodborne
pathogens as well.
[music]
Now let's take a look at what OSHA's
bloodborne pathogen regulation requires
of your facility. The first step
involves the creation of an exposure
control plan. This plan spells out how
your facility will address the
requirements of the regulation itself
and includes a determination [music] of
each employees potential for exposure to
bloodborne pathogens and an examination
of ways to limit or eliminate these
exposures.
The exposure control plan also deals
with setting up a hepatitis B [music]
vaccination program as well as
procedures to be followed whenever an
accidental exposure occurs.
Other parts of the plan address [music]
warning signs and labels, employee
training, and keeping records regarding
exposure, vaccination, [music]
and training.
The plan must also incorporate the use
of standard precautions which require
that all human blood and other body
[music] substances be treated as if they
are known to be infectious.
For people in the health care industry,
one of the most critical issues the
exposure control plan addresses [music]
is how to reduce the risk of
needlesticks and other sharps injuries.
The Centers for Disease Control
estimates that contaminated sharps cause
nearly 400,000 injuries to health care
personnel each year.
When these injuries involve infectious
agents such as hepatitis or HIV, the
affected workers are almost always at
risk of contracting some bloodborne
disease. One of the things OSHA has done
to help combat the danger of needle
sticks is to mandate that exposure
control plans be re-evaluated at least
once a year.
A major focus of these reviews is to
make sure that your facility is using
every means available to keep you safe.
As a rule, the review must confirm that
the exposure control plan reflects
changes in technology that can eliminate
or reduce exposure to bloodborne
pathogens. [music]
Documents the investigation and
implementation of new medical devices
[music]
that are designed to reduce or eliminate
occupational exposure to bloodborne
pathogens.
and incorporates the opinions of
frontline employees whose interactions
with patients expose them to potentially
contaminated sharps. If you would like
to look at your facility's exposure
control plan, see your supervisor
for that there.
[music]
Now, let's take a closer look at the
most important parts of an exposure
control plan. Labeling is the most
visible requirement in the regulation.
Containers carrying any potentially
infectious materials such as blood or
tissue must be marked with a biohazard
label. Biohazard labels must also appear
on any equipment and materials that are
suspected of being contaminated.
The word contaminated indicates the
presence or anticipated presence of
potentially infectious materials on an
item or surface.
Biohazard labels are fluorescent orange
red with a biohazard symbol in a
contrasting color. The word biohazard is
also marked on the lower portion of the
label. Red bags or red containers can
substitute for these labels.
There are several exceptions to these
labeling requirements. Individual
containers of blood do not have to be
labeled if they are placed inside
another labeled container for transport
or storage. And facilities that are
following standard precautions in
handling all specimens do not have to
use this type of labeling if the
specimens are recognizable by the
employees who normally handle them.
Labeled blood products released for
transfusion or other clinical use are
also exempt as long as these specimens
remain in the facility. Common places
that you will see biohazard labels
include refrigerators and freezers
containing blood or other potentially
infectious materials.
Containers used to store, transport or
ship these materials. Contaminated
equipment [music] awaiting cleaning and
containers of regulated waste. In this
case, regulated waste refers to several
things, including potentially infectious
materials such as blood, items such as
used bandages and dressings,
contaminated bedding, and towels.
Contaminated sharps, including needles,
scalpel blades, and broken glass, are
also considered to be regulated waste.
So are containers that may have had
infectious material in them.
Your employer has compiled lists of job
classifications and activities that may
present a risk of exposure to bloodborne
pathogens. These lists can be found in
your facility's exposure control plan.
[music]
[music]
There are many ways that you and your
employer can work to reduce your
exposure to bloodborne pathogens. They
include the use of standard precautions,
remembering to treat all blood and body
substances [music] as if they are
infectious,
engineering controls, following safe
work practices, the use of personal
protective equipment, and appropriate
housekeeping practices.
Engineering controls refer to equipment
or machinery that can minimize exposure.
Your facility [music] uses many of these
already, such as punctureresistant
sharps containers, self- ventilating
laboratory hoods, and sharps with
engineered injury protections such as
self-shaving needles.
Safe work practices [music]
reduce the potential for exposure by
focusing on the safest ways to perform
tasks. Handashing [music] is one of the
most important.
If you have been involved in a situation
where you may have been exposed to
bloodborne pathogens, [music]
OSHA requires that you wash your hands
immediately after removing any gloves
and personal [music] protective
equipment that you are wearing.
When you're finished, remember to use
your towel to turn off the faucet. That
way, you won't recontaminate yourself on
a surface you touched before you washed
your hands. You must also rinse your
eyes, nose, or [music] other mucous
membranes with generous amounts of water
if they have been exposed.
Other work practices are also addressed
by OSHA. For instance, the regulation
stresses [music] the need to minimize
any splashing, spraying, or creation of
droplets when you're dealing with
[music] potentially infectious samples.
And no mouth pipe heading or suctioning
is permitted.
[music]
[music]
OSHA considers housekeeping practices to
be very important to the control of
exposure situations. Written cleaning
schedules specifying the methods of
decontamination that are being used must
be maintained to asssure that all areas
are clean and sanitary.
If they are obviously contaminated, work
surfaces must be cleaned immediately
with an appropriate disinfectant.
Otherwise, this should be done at the
end of each work [music] shift.
Broken glassear is not to be picked up
by hand, but by using a brush and dust
pan, tongs, or other tools.
There are several safe work practices
that must be followed [music] regarding
contaminated needles and sharps. They
must not be bent. They cannot be
recapped or removed unless there is no
feasible alternative. If they have to be
recapped or removed, you must use a
one-handed technique or a mechanical
[music] device. Contaminated
sharps must be discarded as soon as
possible [music] into appropriately
labeled containers that are closable,
puncture resistant, and leakproof.
These containers must be easily
accessible, left upright, replaced
routinely, and never overfilled.
They must be closed when handled, and
are subject to the same secondary
container [music]
requirements as specimens.
Rules also govern the handling of
potentially infectious [music] body
substances and regulated waste.
Regulated waste includes contaminated
personal protective equipment, bandages,
[music] linens, or other materials that

[Music]
there is a lot of talk these days about
HIV and AIDS hbv or Hepatitis B virus
and the dangers of getting infected by
coming into contact with someone else's
blood
in your profession you can face many
situations that could potentially cause
you to come in contact with blood or
body fluids from other individuals
whether it's removing trash that
contains a used syringe handling laundry
soiled with blood or simply cleaning up
after a sick child the precautions you
follow for handling these procedures
could mean preventing serious illness or
even death
that's why OSHA the occupational safety
and health administration has developed
the blood-borne pathogen standard to
provide guidelines that will help you
eliminate or at least reduce your
exposure to hbv HIV and other
blood-borne pathogens while in the
workplace
this video which is included in betco's
University training courses focuses on
OSHA's bloodborne pathogen standard for
the workplace
this video will cover what are
bloodborne pathogens who is covered by
the OSHA bloodborne pathogen standard
what is exposure following universal
precautions protective practices what if
exposure occurs hbv symptoms HIV
symptoms and employer responsibilities
betco has over 300 specialty cleaning
products and a full line of equipment
and accessories
prior to using any cleaning chemical be
sure that you read the label and consult
the safety data sheet for that product
before going any further let's provide a
definition for bloodborne pathogens
blood-borne pathogens are pathogenic
microorganisms that are present in human
blood and can cause disease in humans
these pathogens include but are not
limited to Hepatitis B virus HPV and
human immunodeficiency virus HIV
associated with AIDS
OSHA originally developed the
blood-borne standard for health care and
hospital employees but it has been
expanded to include any occupation in
which reasonably anticipated contact
with blood or other potentially
infectious materials may occur including
someone who may be responsible for the
cleanup of blood or body fluids or even
those who remove trash or handle laundry
Within These settings there may be
potentially infectious materials and how
you take care of them can literally make
the difference between life and death
most occupational exposure to bloodborne
pathogens occurs when the pathogen comes
in contact with the employee's mucous
membranes like the nose or mouth or
breaks in the skin like needle sticks
human bites Cuts or abrasions body
fluids such as blood vomit and in some
instances saliva can potentially contain
blood-borne pathogens but you can easily
protect yourself from coming into
contact with the fluids by following
universal precautions the Centers for
Disease Control and prevention establish
the Universal precaution approach
recommending that blood and certain body
fluids from all patients be considered
potentially infectious and that
infection control precautions be taken
to minimize the risk of exposure this is
the approach taken by OSHA in the
blood-borne standard
the best defense is a thorough offense
always follow universal precautions as
well as your facility's exposure control
plan when handling contaminated
materials
this means that at all times assume that
all blood and most body fluids are
contaminated with blood-borne pathogens
and that you should follow proper
protective practices when handling a
cleanup or an exposure alternative color
coding or labeling of laundry is
acceptable if all of the soiled laundry
is handled using universal precautions
and a labeling or color coding is
sufficient to let all employees know
that compliance with universal
precautions is required if laundry is
shipped to a location that does not use
universal precautions the bags or
containers must be properly labeled and
color-coded red or orange remember that
needles or other sharp objects may be
hidden within the laundry wear personal
protective gear if you are responsible
for handling contaminated laundry
besides protecting yourself you are
responsible for containing the
blood-borne pathogens and
decontaminating the area so someone else
isn't exposed it is crucial to clean and
disinfect the area with the appropriate
disinfectant cleaner
after a cleanup procedure always remove
and dispose of your gloves and other
equipment in a properly labeled
container or a red or orange infectious
waste back
thoroughly wash your hands with a hand
cleaner immediately after you remove the
gloves goggles or other personal
protective equipment good hand washing
helps reduce the spread of infection and
disease
all containers and cleaning equipment
such as mop buckets and tongs used
during decontamination must be
disinfected following use
if there is any chance that you have
been exposed to bloodborne pathogens
contact your supervisor immediately for
specific instructions on exposure
protocol also notify your physician once
an exposure occurs be sure to pay
attention to your health and watch for
any symptoms that are related to HIV or
hbv
Hepatitis B or hbv is a type of liver
disease that inflames the liver and
leads to liver damage and sometimes even
liver cancer
HPV has the following symptoms
fatigue abdominal pain loss of appetite
nausea jaundice vomiting diarrhea
light-colored stools and dark urine
HPV symptoms may not appear for some
time after initial exposure notify your
health care provider immediately if you
think you may be at risk for HPV
Hepatitis B vaccinations must be made
available at no cost to all employees
who have occupational exposure
vaccinations must be provided after
initial blood-borne pathogen training
and within 10 working days of any
assignment which could result in
occupational exposure
if someone should contract HIV they may
develop AIDS or acquired immune
deficiency syndrome
symptoms of HIV infection could include
constant fatigue sore throat persistent
fever persistent rash of Unknown Origin
night sweats persistent swollen glands
mild to severe flu-like symptoms just
like hbv HIV symptoms may not appear for
many years after the exposure if you
think you may be at risk for HIV contact
your health care provider immediately
OSHA requires that each job site in
which there is a reasonable likelihood
of blood-borne pathogen exposure have a
written exposure control plan and it
must be kept updated
reviewing the plan at least annually is
an important part of knowing how to
protect yourself your supervisor should
provide a copy upon request
OSHA requires specific documentation
from your employer when an exposure
occurs your employer must maintain
certain records for three years after
the exposure
now that you understand OSHA's concern
for your health and safety take time to
see how your employer has responded to
the challenge
you may want to read your facility's
written exposure plan
always take universal precautions when
there's a chance you could be exposed to
bloodborne pathogens
remember these protective practices when
you're facing blood-borne pathogen
concerns
always wear personal protective
equipment
never eat drink smoke or apply lip balm
while in areas in which there's a
possibility of bloodborne pathogen
exposure
never manually compress trash
avoid splashing or spattering when
cleaning up never reuse towels or
sponges
use spatulas absorbance or tongs for
cleanup when possible
handle contaminated laundry cautiously
use properly labeled or color-coded
containers and bags when disposing of or
transporting materials contaminated with
bloodborne pathogens this includes
gloves laundry and equipment
always decontaminate surfaces and or
areas with bet Coke disinfectants
always properly wash your hands
disinfect equipment and materials used
for cleanup and if you think you may
have been exposed to bloodborne
pathogens contact your supervisor and
physician immediately
if you need more information ask your
supervisor or check out the OSHA website
at
www.osha.gov you can also contact your
Regional OSHA Office
remember you play an important role in
preventing or reducing contact with
bloodborne pathogens to others as well
as yourself
be proud that you and your employer have
taken the time to learn more about the
OSHA bloodborne standard and use your
knowledge to make a difference in
creating a safe clean and healthy
environment
employees in a healthcare setting have
an even greater risk of exposure to
bloodborne pathogens here are some
additional guidelines developed for your
protection
do not Bend recap or remove contaminated
needles and other contaminated sharps
put contaminated reusable sharps in
designated containers until they can be
properly reprocessed these containers
must be puncture resistant labeled or
color-coded
proof on the sides and bottom regularly
inspect and decontaminate all bins pails
and other containers that may have come
into contact with infectious waste such
as needle bins or trash receptacles of
course follow universal precautions and
dispose of all regulated waste according
to all applicable local state and
federal regulations for infectious waste
disposal if you need more information
ask your supervisor or check out the
OSHA website at
www.osha.gov for more information please
visit
www.betco.com or call 888 gobetco
[Music]

metadata.shortDescription:
This is a demo of our online OSHA-compliant Bloodborne Pathogen Training.  The training is one hour long.  The demo shows lesson 1 of 6.  The full course is available for purchase at: 

http://www.bloodbornepathogentraining.com

This training is for anyone who comes into contact with blood as part of their assigned job duties.  This includes:

1) Healthcare staff such as physicians, nurses, etc
2) Healthcare housekeeping personel, emergency resonders such as paramedics, firefighters, and emergency medical technicians
3) Mortitians,
4) Dentists
5) Teachers/school staff
6) Tattoo and body piercing artists

segments.text: OSHA blood-borne pathogen training
this course addresses the occupational
exposure to blood-borne pathogens
standard OSHA's blood-borne pathogens is
a federal osha standard that prescribes
safeguards to protect workers against
the health hazards from exposure to
blood and other potentially infectious
materials and to reduce their risk from
this exposure
Table of Contents lesson one
introduction to blood-borne pathogens
get ready you are now ready to start the
course press lesson one introduction to
blood-borne pathogens lesson outline
introduction to blood-borne pathogens
what is a blood-borne pathogen
blood-borne pathogens are microorganisms
such as viruses or bacteria that are
present in human blood and that can
cause disease in humans these pathogens
include but are not limited to hepatitis
B HPV hepatitis C HCV human
immunodeficiency virus HIV malaria
Vasili osis syphilis West Nile virus
other potentially infectious materials
in addition to human blood blood-borne
pathogens can also be found in other
potentially infectious materials
including the following body fluids
especially because of their potential to
be contaminated with blood blood
products such as plasma or serum saliva
and dental procedures semen vaginal
secretions skin tissue and/or cell
cultures any other bodily fluid that is
visibly contaminated with blood the
following body fluids are not expected
to be infectious sources of blood-borne
pathogens unless they are visibly
contaminated with blood vomit tears
sweat urine feces sputum nasal
secretions note since you may not always
be able to tell whether a bodily fluid
has been mixed with blood it is best to
treat all bodily fluids as potentially
dangerous transmission of blood-borne
pathogens blood-borne pathogens can be
transmitted when infectious blood or
other potentially infectious material is
introduced into the bloodstream of a
person transmission of blood-borne
pathogens in the workplace can occur
through infected blood or other
potentially infectious materials being
introduced through non-intact skin acne
scratches cuts bites blisters or wounds
contact with mucous membranes found in
the eye nose or mouth contaminated
sharps or needle injuries the need for a
safety standard osha estimates that 8
million workers in the healthcare
industry and related occupations are at
risk of occupational exposure to
blood-borne pathogens including but not
limited to HIV the virus that causes
AIDS hepatitis B and hepatitis C
according to the Centers for Disease
Control
100,000 Americans have died from AIDS
and over 1 million Americans are
infected with HIV about 65 cases of HIV
infection due to occupational exposure
occur each year about 8700 health care
workers are infected with hepatitis B
each year about 200 health care workers
die from hepatitis B each year one
milliliter of blood can contain over 100
million infectious doses of hepatitis B
virus 60 to 70 percent of the
individuals infected with hepatitis C
virus show no discernible symptoms
according to the Centers for Disease
Control and Prevention hepatitis C virus
infection is the most common chronic
blood-borne infection in the US
the OSHA blood-borne pathogens standard
OSHA published the occupational exposure
to blood-borne pathogens standard on
December 6 1991 the purpose of the
standard is to protect workers by
limiting occupational exposure to blood
and other potentially infectious
materials in 2000 the needle stick
safety and Prevention Act public law
1:06 - four-30 mandated that osha
clarify and revise the blood-borne
pathogens standard to address the
implementation of safer needle devices
osha published the revised standard in
the Federal Register in January 2001 the
revised standard became effective in
April 2001 the blood-borne pathogen
standard is located in title 29 of the
Code of Federal Regulations 29 CFR 19
who is covered by the standard all
employees who could be reasonably
anticipated to face contact with blood
or other potentially infectious
materials as the result of performing
their assigned job duties are covered by
the blood-borne pathogen standards
this list shows examples of some of the
professions at risk of occupational
exposure to blood-borne pathogens
let's take a quiz to review what you've
learned
you
end of demo thank you for going through
the blood-borne pathogen training demo
if you would like more information
please contact us at telephone five one
two four zero two five nine six three or
email sales at blood-borne pathogen
training.com also for more information
please be sure and visit our frequently
asked questions page
