metadata.title: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Spill Cleanup Training
metadata.author: Training Videos

segments.text: Welcome to the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens
spill cleanup training. This video will
guide you through the standard protocols
for managing spills in an industrial
setting in accordance with OSHA
regulation 29 CFR 1,910.1030.
As an employee who may encounter blood
or potentially infectious materials, it
is mandatory that you receive this
training upon your initial assignment
and annually. I am Zafara and I will be
your guide as we review the proper
procedures for handling an incident
safely.
The golden rule of BBP safety is to
always use universal precautions. Never
assume a spill is harmless based on
appearance. Treat all human blood and
bodily fluids as if they are known to be
highly infectious and always exercise
maximum caution.
It is important to understand your
hazards. Bloodborne pathogens include
viruses like hepatitis B, hepatitis C,
and HIV. Other potentially infectious
materials or OPIM, such as urine or
vomit, are considered hazards only when
they are visibly contaminated with
blood.
Every BBP spill kit contains four
essential components. an EPA registered
disinfectant, absorbent material, tools
for handling sharps, and proper disposal
supplies like biohazard bags and sharps
containers. Locate these kits in your
zone so you are prepared to act.
Proper personal protective equipment is
your biological barrier. This includes
face protection, disposable nitro or
vinyl gloves, a gown or apron if there
is a risk of splashing, and shoe covers
to prevent the spread of contaminants
across the factory floor.
The spill cleanup protocol follows eight
essential steps. It is critical that you
follow these exactly. Skipping any part
of this process can compromise the
safety of the entire facility.
Steps one and two are to secure the area
and suit up. Block off the spill site
immediately and have a co-worker stand
guard to prevent traffic. Then ensure
you are fully equipped with your PPE
before approaching.
Step three is to remove sharps first.
Never pick up broken glass or needles
with your hands, even with gloves.
Always use mechanical tools and place
them directly into a rigid,
punctureproof sharps container.
Step four is to contain the spill. If
available, pour absorbent powder over
the liquid to turn it into a gel. If
using towels, gently lay them over the
spill. Do not smash or stomp on them, as
this can cause dangerous splashing.
Step five is to pick up the debris. Use
a disposable scraper or cardboard to
carefully scoop up the material, working
from the outside edges inward. Place all
waste directly into the red biohazard
bag.
Step six is applying the disinfectant,
which is the most frequently missed
step. Spray the area and wait for the
required contact time listed on the
bottle. It must remain visibly wet for
this duration to effectively kill
viruses.
Step seven is to wipe up and do your
PPE. After the contact time has elapsed,
wipe the area with paper towels. When
removing your gloves, do so carefully by
turning them inside out to trap
contaminants within.
Step eight is to wash your hands
immediately. Scrub with soap and warm
water for at least 20 seconds. Remember
that hand sanitizer is only a temporary
measure and does not replace thorough
washing.
If an exposure incident occurs, wash the
affected area immediately and flush eyes
or mouth for 15 minutes. Inform a
manager right away so the company can
provide a free confidential medical
evaluation and follow-up treatment.
Module 5 covers your rights and
responsibilities. These include
receiving the hepatitis B vaccine series
at no cost, access to the exposure
control plan, and having fully stocked
PPE kits available. In return, you must
follow universal precautions and
promptly report any exposure incidents.
Regarding the mandatory hepatitis B
protocol, employers must offer the
vaccine series free of charge by day 10
of your assignment. You have the right
to accept the series or formally decline
by signing a waiver, though you may
change your mind at any time.
You have a right to know about facility
hazards. You may access the written
exposure control plan at any time.
Furthermore, your medical and exposure
records are kept confidential and you
are entitled to request access to your
own files without fear of reprisal.
For trainers, OSHA compliance requires
that BBP training be interactive. You
must maintain documentation, including
dates and attendee names on file for 3
years. Always conduct a sightspecific
walkthrough to ensure new hires know
exactly where kits and the exposure
control plan are located.
To practice, use the shaving cream test.
Apply cream to the palms to simulate a
pathogen. Then remove gloves. If hands
remain clean, the pinch and peel
technique was perfect. If cream touches
the skin, the technique was flawed and
must be corrected.
Thank you for completing this training.
By following these protocols, you help
maintain a safe, compliant, and healthy
industrial environment. Please reach out
to your supervisor if you have further
questions regarding bloodborne pathogen
safety.

metadata.title: Bloodborne Pathogens for Custodians
metadata.author: SafetyTrainingNetwork.com
metadata.shortDescription:
Maintenance and custodial workers regularly encounter situations where they could be exposed to a bloodborne pathogen. This video, produced especially for custodian and maintenance staff, demonstrates how custodians and maintenance workers can safely clean up spills of blood or other potentially infectious materials without risking exposure.

Topics covered also include:
•What bloodborne pathogens are
•Diseases that could be transmitted
•Potential exposure routes
•How to protect yourself from exposure

12 min, 2010, Training Network
DVD $299.95
 
Want to preview the entire video? Find it on our website, www.safetytrainingnetwork.com:

metadata.title: OSHA in Healthcare: Key Safety Standards, Bloodborne Pathogens, PPE & Workplace Safety Explained
metadata.author: nurselyf
metadata.shortDescription:
From bloodborne pathogen exposure to workplace violence and PPE protocols, OSHA plays a vital role in protecting healthcare workers on the front lines. In this video, we break down the essential OSHA regulations healthcare staff need to understand, including how hospitals stay compliant and how workers can advocate for their own safety.

📌 In This Video, You’ll Learn:
✅ What OSHA is and how it regulates safety in healthcare settings
✅ Key details of the Bloodborne Pathogen Standard
✅ OSHA’s guidelines on sharps safety, chemical hazards, and PPE use
✅ How employers prevent workplace injuries and violence
✅ Ways healthcare teams maintain OSHA compliance through training and audits

Find more in-depth nursing insights in my books on Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/author/ramrengel

📌 #OSHAinHealthcare #WorkplaceSafety #BloodbornePathogens #NursingEducation #PPETraining #HealthcareCompliance #InfectionControl #JASlyf #HealthAdvocatesOfAmerica

exposure control plan. Provide free

precautions. Supply appropriate PPE,

engineering controls like sharps,
containers, and safety needles. Document
and follow up on all exposure incidents.

patient handling programs to reduce back

Personal protective equipment and

proper fit testing for N95 masks, use of
eye protection and proper dawning and

scenarios. How healthcare settings stay
OSHA compliant? Annual training on all

and safety drills, incident reporting

a safety officer or infection control
lead. OSHA compliance isn't just about

culture of safety that puts worker
protection front and center. Bottom

but it should never be dangerous because

metadata.title: 1099 Contractors vs W-2 Employees - How to Classify Your Workers
metadata.author: CSI Accounting
metadata.shortDescription:
Struggling to determine whether your workers should be classified as W-2 employees or 1099 independent contractors? In this video, we'll break down the key differences between these two categories and guide you through the process of classifying your workers correctly.

We'll cover:

- The critical distinctions between W-2 employees and 1099 independent contractors.
- The IRS's 'Three Factor Test' and other guidelines to help you make informed decisions on worker classification.
- The potential risks and consequences of misclassifying your workers, including fines, penalties, and legal issues.

Don't leave your business exposed to risks and complications. Watch this video to gain a better understanding of worker classification and ensure compliance with IRS guidelines. Subscribe to our channel for more insightful videos on business management and financial matters!

metadata.title: W2 vs 1099: How I Built a Remote Cleaning Team Without Payroll Headaches
metadata.author: Jon Margalit
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you wondering if you should hire W2 employees or 1099 contractors for your cleaning business? In this video, I explain the W2 vs 1099 cleaners debate and how I built a 7-figure remote cleaning business using only 1099 contractors. You will learn how to hire cleaners the right way, avoid payroll taxes, stay compliant, and build a cleaning business system that scales without the stress of employees.

I share why 1099 cleaners work better for most cleaning business owners, how to set up a cleaning company that is profitable and tax efficient, and the steps to grow a cleaning business with systems and automation. If you want to start a cleaning business, grow a cleaning business, or run a house cleaning business that brings real freedom, this video is full of proven cleaning business tips and strategies.

👉 Want my free step-by-step guide on how to get your first remote cleaning client, without paying for ads or knocking on doors?
Download it here: https://jonmargalit.com/youtube?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=bio

📘 Jon's Remote Cleaning Business Course (steal Jon's systems): YouTube https://jonmargalit.com/youtube?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=bio
I cover all of the topics you need to master:  Legal & Finance / Branding / Staffing / Sales & Customer Service / Marketing / Advertising / Customer Acquisition (organic and paid) / Website Design / Automation & Apps / Pricing Guide and much, much more…

🔵 ABOUT

How To Launch A Profitable House Cleaning Business in Just 30 Days—No Experience Needed!

Rags to Riches University is your blueprint to launching a profitable remote house cleaning business without ever needing to handle the cleaning yourself. My step-by-step program tailored for beginners is designed for rapid implementation and success. With clear, concise, and actionable videos, you can get your business off the ground in 2 weeks and start seeing profits within 30 days. Our streamlined approach is designed for a quick and affordable setup with rapid monetization.

This channel provides you with all the insights, tips, and hacks, in a simple how-to format so you can easily learn how to make a minimum of $10,000/month by starting and growing a house cleaning business. 

I cover all of the topics you need to master:  Legal & Finance / Branding / Staffing / Sales & Customer Service / Marketing / Advertising / Customer Acquisition (organic and paid) / Website Design / Automation & Apps / Pricing Guide and much, much more…

this disclaimer. I'm not an attorney,

But, let's clear something up first. W2
and 1099 aren't just tax codes. They
represent two completely different
relationships. W2 employee means that
you control how they do the job. You
provide the tools. You dictate the
schedule. You're responsible for taxes,
insurance, unemployment, etc. 1099
contractor means that you control how
the work gets done. They use their own
supplies. They can accept or decline
jobs. You don't manage them. You partner
with them. Now, the IRS uses something
called common law tests to figure out if
someone's a contractor or not. And that
basically boils down to one question.
Who has control? If you're telling your
cleaner when to show up, what supplies
to use, how to do the job, and you're
the one providing everything, that's a
W2 relationship, even if you call it
something else. And most cleaning
business owners get this wrong. They
want the tax advantages of 1099, but
they treat their cleaners like
employees. They assign specific
schedules, they give them supplies, they
require uniforms, and they tell them
exactly how to clean, and then they're
shocked when the state comes knocking.
Now, here's the thing that's
interesting. I built my team using a
different model, one that gives me the
benefits of working with contractors,
but keeps me out of trouble. I run my
company like a network. Cleaners don't
work for me. They partner with my brand.
They bring their own supplies and tools,
and they clean how they want, as long as
the end result meets my standard. They
decide if they want to take the jobs or
not. But here's the key difference. I
structured it that way on purpose
because I don't want to control. I want
alignment. Now, I want to be clear
again. I'm not giving legal advice and
you should always talk to your
accountant or your employment attorney.
But I will tell you this. I've built the
system that keeps me in compliant, keeps
taxes and liabilities low, and gives
contractors freedom while still creating
a consistent customer experience. But
here's the part nobody talks about. This
model isn't just better for me, it's
better for the cleaners. I'm not trying
to create employees. I'm trying to
create independent business owners,
people who take pride in their work
because it's their business, not just a
job. When someone joins my network,
they're not just cleaning houses.
They're building something for
themselves. They get the freedom to
choose their schedule. They decide how
much work they want and they feel
empowered. And because they're 1099s,
they get access to real tax benefits
that employees never see. Most of them
don't even know this until I explain it.
But as a 1099, they can write off things
like gas and mileage, vehicle
maintenance, cleaning supplies and
equipment, uniforms, meals while they
work, cell phone bill, even a portion of
their rent if they use it as a home
office. That's not just a perk, it's a
strategy. Some of the cleaners in my
network end up paying almost nothing in
taxes because they're structured like
actual small business owners. That's
what they are and it's totally legal.
They're running a solo business under my
umbrella. I give them the platform, the
jobs, and the support, but they own the
hustle and the outcome. And that's
ownership. That's why they take pride in
their work. That's why my customer
experience is better than most companies
that have employees. Because when people
feel like owners, they show up
differently. And by the way, if you're
getting value, please subscribe and like
my channel so I create more content like
this. I do my best to help each and
every one of you as much as possible.
And I post new videos every week about
how to build, automate, and grow a
profitable cleaning business. All right,
so now you might be wondering, if
they're not employees, how do you ensure
quality? And that's a great question.
Just because I don't manage them doesn't
mean I don't have standards. I have
systems and I have checklists. The
people who follow the process get more
work. The ones who don't fall off
naturally. That's not control. That's
market forces. And the best part, it
makes my business scalable because I'm
not holding on to every cleaner. I'm
empowering people who actually want to
work. This is where the industry is
heading. Not just in cleaning, but
across all home services because people
want jobs. They don't want
opportunities. The people who follow the
process get more work. And the ones who
don't, they fall off naturally. That's
not control. That's market forces. And
the best part, it makes my business
scalable because I'm not holding on to
every cleaner. I'm empowering people who
actually want to do the work. That's
what I figured out. And that's why I
teach this now to other cleaning
business owners inside my training
program. If you're trying to build a
cleaning business and you're stuck on
that W2 versus 1099 debate, here's the
truth. There's a way to do it right. You
don't need to hire W2 employees. You
don't need to hand out vacuums and
micromanage people. You need a system
that makes cleaners want to work with
you, not feel like they have to. If you
want to see how I do it step by step,
you can access my training today at my
website, johnmargleite.com. The links in
the description. So, stop trying to
control people and start building
leverage. Because employees are
overhead, but contractors are freedom if
you do it right.

your business a little bit longer than you thought you would whenever the startup is starting to ramp up you are typically required to be able to demonstrate you have at least $50,000 in liquid assets that's cash stocks bonds you can sell immediately in order to have cash on hand that $50,000 is usually a standard requirement in the territory franchise model then you also have the net worth requirement you got to be able to at least demonstrate that you have $100,000 of net worth to your name and just to be clear net worth is assets like your house any property that you own any land that you own even businesses that you own minus your debts so it has to have a difference of $100,000 it doesn't mean that that's all cash your cash does count towards that but it doesn't mean all that has to be 100,000 cash it's just if your house is worth $500,000 and then your debt on it is $400,000 you have $100,000 net worth but if you also have $50,000 cash then technically you have $150,000 of net worth so it's really important to know that you're financially stable so that when you do become a franchisee you can weather any of the business storms you might face during your startup now obviously a territory franchisees there to help you dodge as many of those storms as possible and to make you build and help you build your business as fast as you can so what's The Upfront investment typically for these you can actually go check out service Master's website they've got updated numbers you can check out office Prides franchise opportunity website you can always reach out to us at asset.com to get everything that you need in order to know what The Upfront investment cost is but typically depending on the territory size and how much marketing you want to do you're looking at investing at least $40,000 to upwards of $150,000 now that's extremely rare to end up up there unless you're going to be taking on an entire city like Denver Colorado for example or Atlanta Georgia but most areas or smaller or average territories are going to require you to spend $150 ,000 to get your business off the ground but you are likely going to need to be ready to be able to spend $40,000 cash to get your business going so anywhere in between that is what you're looking at investing again compared to unit franchises these are a lot more of an investment but that's why the ongoing costs are extremely important to understand because it's going to help us have an idea of how big of a business we can get and how profitable that business can be so here's the main differentiator between you unit franchises and territory franchises territory franchises have a lot more favorable fee structure typically royalties start around 9 or 10% our starts at 7% it just depends on which brand you're looking at and then at certain Revenue levels that royalty actually drops I know that in ours we like to incentivize our franchisees to grow and grow and grow and it actually doesn't cost us as much to help support them and carry all the systems and keep the website going for them it doesn't cost us as much as they grow so we actually drop and decrease our royalty as a franchisee gets larger so we like to have some rewards built in there and I know other brands do something similar as well as opposed to unit franchises where it's always the same no matter how big your business gets then most territory franchises have two more smaller fees one is called the brand marketing fund contribution or national brand fund contribution this is what the company uses to do National advertising or follow-up campaigns online and things like that this is typically going to run between a half% and 2% of Revenue collected and then you have What's called the technology fee this covers things like the software and any email addresses and any technology that helps make the business run smoother on the backend for the franchises ours is currently at $35 per week and this is typically a pretty low weekly fee compared to other things like the unit franchise with all those extra fees on top but the reason for lower fees here in the territory franchise is because the franchisee has been trained to build a company they've been trained to build a business and it's up to them to grow it whereas a unit franchise they're out there to selling the business investing ahead of time for their franchisees but then having to sell them the accounts in order to make up their costs and collect their fees to build their profit so a territory franchise requires you to be responsible it does give you a lot of support gives you a ton of upfront training sometimes up to 2 weeks you're invited to an office and you can go and train live you can do training virtually either way it's up to you to build your business with the knowledge systems and tools that you're given whenever you have a territory franchise and the neat thing about a territory franchise is that you can grow your business as big as you want it and you can hire whoever you want to run it as opposed to a unit franchise it's a lot more difficult to hire people profitably to help clean your accounts because you have so many fees as opposed to a territory franchise where the fees are actually decreasing as you get bigger to help you be more efficient you can hire in managers to run your business you can pay your cleaners really well and keep them longer and have all kinds of benefits to building a company as opposed to owning a job now as you can tell I do favor this model but again I'll admit it's not for everybody personally I have owned two franchises that are are territory franchises they were both cleaning related they weren't commercial cleaning specifically but I've been a franchisee twice and I still own one of them right now as a side business so who is a territory commercial cleaning franchise good for and who's it not good for the person that a territory franchise is good for is someone who wants to learn how to build a business maybe they haven't built a business before this is their first time being a business owner they're coming out of the corporate world they want to make that jump into entrepreneurship but they want someone to hold their hand and give them a business model that works and that's proven and that's profitable or it's somebody who has had some business experience whether they worked for somebody else or they tried building their own it didn't go the way they thought they wanted it to go and they want to learn the systems and how to really build a company right then they can go into a franchise learn that build it up you can even sell it and cash out on it sell it like a house right businesses are extremely valuable once they're cash flowing so you can use this experience to learn how to build a business Advance your career Advance your financial life and meet your goals and then go on to build other things or like I've done I'm still hanging on to one of the franchises that I own and it pretty much runs itself so you can set it up however you want to do it when it comes to a territory franchise now who's it not good for it's not good for somebody who does not want to submit to the systems or the way that things things have been proven to be done it's not good for somebody who already knows how to build a company on their own they may have already built several multi-million dollar companies and they don't really need to learn how to do this that kind of person is totally fine starting their own business on their own or if it's somebody that is just confident in themselves they don't really want to pay The Upfront investment and the ongoing royalties in either a unit franchise or a territory franchise and metadata.title: Own a Cleaning Franchise Without Cleaning? Stratus Clean Master Franchise Explained
metadata.author: Franchise Wizards
metadata.shortDescription:
What if you could own a business in the $100 billion cleaning industry WITHOUT doing the cleaning yourself?

In this episode of the *Franchise Wizards Podcast*, Sheila and Daniel Purim interview *Rob Lancit, VP of Franchise Development at Stratus Clean*, to explore one of franchising's most unique opportunities: the *Master Franchise model*.

Stratus Clean has been recognized by Entrepreneur magazine as the *#1 Fastest-Growing Franchise for four consecutive years*, ranking #1 in commercial cleaning and #21 overall in the 2026 Franchise 500.

Unlike a traditional commercial cleaning franchise, Stratus Master Franchise Owners develop an exclusive territory, recruit Unit Franchisees, secure commercial cleaning contracts, and support a network of cleaning entrepreneurs.

*The Unit Franchisees do the cleaning. Master Franchise Owners focus on growing the business.*

🚀 *EXPLORE THE STRATUS CLEAN FRANCHISE OPPORTUNITY*

Request more information, explore investment requirements, and check territory availability:

👉 https://franchisewizards.com/podcast/lp/stratusclean

What You'll Discover
✅ *$100 Billion Industry:* Why commercial cleaning is an essential B2B service with recurring demand.

✅ *Master Franchise Explained:* How owners build a regional network of cleaning entrepreneurs without personally performing cleaning services.

✅ *90% Recurring Revenue:* How long-term commercial cleaning contracts support the business model.

✅ *Nine Revenue Streams:* Franchise fees, royalties, contract sales, specialty services, and more.

✅ *Recession-Resistant Industry:* Why commercial cleaning has demonstrated resilience through economic uncertainty and the pandemic, with services that are difficult to replace entirely with AI.

✅ *Scalability & Lifestyle:* How owners can build a transferable business asset while pursuing greater flexibility and work-life balance.

Meet Rob Lancit — Franchise Executive & Author
With nearly 30 years of franchising experience, Rob shares insights into business ownership, leadership, and entrepreneurship.

We also discuss his new book, _Take My Advice, I'm Not Using It: My Life Lessons and the Mistakes I've Made_, and the importance of taking risks, learning from mistakes, and embracing personal growth.

📚 *Get Rob's book:*
https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H9W8SMN7

Explore Franchise Ownership With Franchise Wizards
Not sure which franchise is right for you? Franchise Wizards helps aspiring entrepreneurs discover businesses aligned with their experience, goals, investment preferences, and lifestyle. Our consulting services are complimentary to candidates.

🧙 *Schedule a Complimentary Franchise Consultation:*
https://franchisewizards.com/contact-us

🤖 *Try Our AI Franchise Matchmaking Tool:*
https://franchisewizards.com/vsl3-best-franchises

🌐 Website: https://franchisewizards.com/

*Subscribe to the Franchise Wizards Podcast* for interviews with franchise leaders and insights into entrepreneurship, franchising, and business ownership.

*Disclaimer:* This episode is for informational purposes only and is not an offer to sell a franchise or a guarantee of financial results. Business performance and investment requirements vary. Review the franchisor's current Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD), including Item 19 where applicable, and consult qualified professionals before investing

So the the the master franchisees role essentially the the white collar activities in a blue collar industry. >> Yeah, that's that's absolutely one way to look at it for sure. >> And and one thing that is particularly interesting is that commercial cleaning isn't discretionary service for many businesses. facilities need to be maintained regardless of what's happening in the economy. A lot of times people tend to put us in a box that they understand. And that box most of the time is, well, you clean office buildings. Well, yes, we do. I'm sure you know you and a lot of your listeners were negatively affected during the pandemic, right? And I'm not downplaying that because I know it had a negative effect on people globally. metadata.title: Commercial Cleaning Contracts, Janitorial Franchises Video Presentation With CC
metadata.author: Win Driggins
metadata.shortDescription:
In this presentation, I explore the hidden business model behind commercial cleaning contracts, janitorial franchises, and facility services and explain why this lane is much more than simple mopping, trash removal, and restroom cleaning. While many people think commercial cleaning is just basic custodial labor, the deeper reality is that this lane often operates as a contract-labor, inspection-quality, and account-retention business built around subcontract opportunities, mirror and window-detail cleaning, restroom sanitation, recurring janitorial service menus, franchise investment models, training systems, coordinated cleaning crews, franchisee recognition, facility-service dispatch, specialty floor care, carpet service, light maintenance, after-hours office cleaning, client prospecting, and year-round sanitation demand. This presentation moves from the cleaning-contract opportunity itself, into visible quality-control work, then into janitorial-service packaging, franchise economics, crew deployment, facility-service expansion, specialty work, owner business development, and the final reminder that sanitation and order are needed in every season. It shows that the visible product is a clean building, but the hidden business is managing labor, inspections, upsells, and contract retention at thin margins.

This presentation breaks down how commercial cleaning businesses do more than clean buildings. They turn recurring sanitation needs, labor coordination, inspection pressure, and client expectations into contracts, franchise systems, specialty-service upsells, and renewal risk.

The visible product is a clean building. The hidden business is managing labor, inspections, and contract retention.

metadata.title: How to Bid a Commercial Cleaning Contract: 20,000 Sq Ft Example.
metadata.author: Bid & Profit Lab
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to price a commercial cleaning contract using a fictional 20,000 sq ft office example. We calculate worker-hours, loaded labor costs, monthly expenses, and the bid needed for a 25% margin after including costs.

Get our paid Commercial Cleaning Bid & Margin System:
https://www.etsy.com/listing/4562347967/commercial-cleaning-bid-calculator

In this worked example:
• Monthly modeled cost: $2,100
• Monthly price for a 25% modeled margin: $2,800
• Modeled monthly profit: $700 before income tax
• One extra worker-hour per visit reduces modeled profit to $375

CHAPTERS
00:00 What should you bid?
00:24 Define the cleaning scope
00:53 Calculate worker-hours
01:15 Worker-hours versus crew size
01:34 Visits and monthly labor hours
01:50 Loaded labor cost
02:17 Costs beyond wages
02:56 Price for your target margin
03:12 Check the margin
03:24 Markup versus margin
03:44 Stress-test labor time
04:01 What happens to your profit?
04:26 Spreadsheet preview
04:51 Recap

All rates and allowances are illustrative, not market benchmarks. Replace them with your own service scope, labor requirements, and costs. The product preview shows actual workbook input fields before data entry; the teaching calculations are presented separately.

Bid & Profit Lab sells the spreadsheet linked above. This video provides educational examples, not a guarantee of profit.

segments.text: What should you charge to clean a twenty thousand
square foot office?
The size alone cannot tell you.
In this example, a monthly price of twenty eight
hundred dollars produces a twenty five percent margin after
the costs we include.
But if each visit takes just one extra worker
hour, that margin drops to about thirteen percent.
Let's build the bid so you can see where
those numbers come from.
This is a fictional example, not a recommended price
for your market.
We are assuming twenty thousand cleanable square feet, three
visits a week, and a defined routine office cleaning
scope. Before using any calculation, confirm the rooms, restrooms,
surfaces, tasks and service standards.
Window cleaning, carpet extraction and other periodic work need
their own allowance or a separate quote.
Two buildings with the same area can require very
different amounts of work.
For this example, assume the agreed cleaning scope can
be completed at four thousand square feet per worker
hour. Divide twenty thousand by four thousand.
That gives us five worker hours per visit.
This rate is only a teaching assumption.
Use a walkthrough, your own measured performance and the
actual task list to establish a realistic rate.
Notice that we said worker hours.
One cleaner working five hours uses five worker hours.
Two cleaners working two and a half hours each
also use five worker hours.
Hiring a second person does not automatically double the
labor needed for the same scope.
It changes how you might schedule those hours.
Three visits a week, multiplied by fifty two weeks,
divided by twelve months, gives thirteen visits per month
on average. Your actual service calendar may differ.
Five worker hours per visit times thirteen visits gives
sixty five cleaning hours a month.
Now assume a base wage of twenty dollars an
hour and a payroll burden allowance of twenty five
percent. Multiply twenty dollars by one point two five.
Our loaded labor cost is twenty five dollars per
hour. That burden percentage is another assumption.
Replace it with your own employment costs and avoid
counting the same expense twice.
Sixty five hours at twenty five dollars gives sixteen
hundred and twenty five dollars of monthly cleaning labor.
Wages are not the whole bid.
We will add one hundred dollars for cleaning supplies,
seventy five for equipment, one hundred for travel, one
hundred for separate supervision and one hundred for allocated
overhead. Those allowances total four hundred and seventy five
dollars. They are illustrative, and the travel allowance must
cover the relevant travel costs, including paid time where
applicable. Add that to our cleaning labor and the
modeled monthly cost is twenty one hundred dollars.
If you do the cleaning yourself, include the cost
of your working time.
Leaving your own labor out makes the job look
more profitable than it is.
We want a twenty five percent margin after these
included costs, before income tax.
Divide cost by one minus the target margin.
That is twenty one hundred divided by zero point
seven five, giving a monthly price of twenty eight
hundred dollars. Check it: twenty eight hundred in revenue
minus twenty one hundred in costs leaves seven hundred
dollars. Seven hundred divided by twenty eight hundred equals
twenty five percent.
Adding twenty five percent to cost gives a different
answer. That produces a price of twenty six hundred
and twenty five dollars, with five hundred and twenty
five dollars left over.
Divide that profit by the selling price and the
margin is twenty percent.
Markup is measured against cost.
Margin is measured against revenue.
Before sending the quote, test what happens if your
labor estimate is wrong.
Suppose each visit needs six worker hours instead of
five. Six times thirteen visits gives seventy eight hours.
At twenty five dollars per hour, labor now costs
nineteen hundred and fifty dollars.
Keep our other allowances unchanged and total cost becomes
twenty four hundred and twenty five dollars.
At the same twenty eight hundred dollar price, only
three hundred and seventy five dollars remains.
That is about thirteen point four percent of revenue.
One extra worker hour per visit nearly halves the
modeled profit. A spreadsheet can calculate the result, but
it cannot make an unrealistic time estimate accurate.
The repeatable workflow is scope, labor, full cost, target
margin, then a stress test.
If you prefer a ready made spreadsheet for your
bidding calculations, our Commercial Cleaning Bid and Margin System
is linked in the description.
We sell this tool.
Use your own job assumptions, review the result and
check that every promised service is covered before you
submit a bid.
For this example, the modeled monthly cost is twenty
one hundred dollars, and the price required for a
twenty five percent margin is twenty eight hundred dollars.
Your bid will change with your scope and costs.
Start with realistic worker hours, include the costs beyond
wages, and divide by one minus your target margin.
Then test the estimate before you send it.

Need a simple way to estimate cleaning jobs for your business?

In this tutorial, I'll show you how to use a Google Sheets cleaning business quote calculator to estimate labor costs, supplies, travel expenses, overhead, and your suggested customer price.

- How to enter home size and number of cleaners
- How to compare Standard, Deep Clean, and Move-out cleaning
- How labor and supply costs affect your quote

metadata.title: Best Janitorial & Commercial Cleaning Software 2026
metadata.author: Modern Field Service
metadata.shortDescription:
If you run a commercial cleaning or janitorial business in 2026, finding real software advice is weirdly hard. Almost everything out there is a two-minute vendor ad, or a list of residential maid apps that has nothing to do with contracts, crews, and inspections. So this is the comparison that doesn't really exist yet: Jobber, Connecteam, Swept, Janitorial Manager, and FieldCamp — judged on actual commercial cleaning work, with a winner declared at the end of every section.

First we clear the residential trap. Maid apps are good at what they do, but what they do is houses: book a recurring home clean, remind the customer, collect payment. Commercial cleaning is crews against contracts, the same office five nights a week, and a client who cares about inspections and proof of work — not a booking widget.

Then the sections that actually decide it: janitorial depth (inspections, work loading, proof of service), crew scheduling at 30/50/100 cleaners, communication and automation, and pricing models that aren't remotely comparable — per-hub, per-location, quote-led, and per-seat all in the same category.

One finding worth calling out: I went through every one of these pricing pages, and not one of Swept, Janitorial Manager, Connecteam, Jobber, or Housecall Pro advertises a WhatsApp integration. Swept actually names WhatsApp as the chaos it replaces. If you've ever run night crews, you know that's where your cleaners already are.

00:00 — Why janitorial software advice is so bad

02:00 — Crew scheduling at 30, 50, 100 cleaners
02:58 — Communication & AI: the section nobody covers
03:45 — Pricing: four completely different models
04:28 — The 2026 verdict, by company type
05:1 — The one comparison that decides it

metadata.title: What is a Day Porter?  Expectations vs Reality in Cleaning Businesses | Ep. 31
metadata.author: OctoClean Media
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, we break down everything you need to know about day porters, from what they do daily to the expectations vs. reality that every business owner should understand. With years of experience running a commercial cleaning company, we share our real stories, lessons learned, and what to avoid when hiring day porters.

If you run a cleaning business, janitorial service, or commercial facilities company, this episode is your guide to making smart decisions about day porters.

In this podcast we cover all about Dayporters:
- What to expect when hiring one (and the reality behind it)
- Mistakes to avoid that could cost your business money
- How day porters impact client satisfaction & retention
- Where to start if you’re considering adding day porters to your team

metadata.author: Cleaning Business Tools
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you price a house cleaning job without guessing? In this video I price one example home from scratch (1,800 sq ft, 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms, 10 miles away) and check every step in a spreadsheet calculator.

The method: Price = (labor + supplies + travel) × (1 + markup), then add any add-ons, take off any recurring discount, round up, and never go below your minimum job price.

In the example ($32 per cleaner-hour, 20% markup, $6 supplies, $0.76/mile, $120 minimum):
• 212 minutes = 3.53 labor hours → $113.07 labor
• + $6 supplies + $15.20 round-trip driving = $134.27 cost
• × 1.2 markup = $161.12 → rounds up to $165 (about $30.73 profit, 18.6% margin)
• Biweekly at 10% off → $150. Heavy first clean → $220. + inside oven → $270
• A 700 sq ft apartment works out to about $75 by cost, so the $120 minimum applies

All numbers are examples. Use your own wage, costs and time standards, and time your own cleans.

The spreadsheet in this video is my own product, the Cleaning Business Pricing Calculator (Excel .xlsx):

What’s the difference between General Liability Insurance and Workers’ Compensation Insurance for a business?

These are two of the most common business insurance policies, but they cover completely different types of claims — and most businesses need both.

In this video, we break down the basics of General Liability vs Workers’ Comp insurance in simple terms and explain how each policy works.

🔹 What General Liability insurance covers
🔹 What Workers Compensation insurance covers
🔹 Third-party injuries vs employee injuries
🔹 Common examples of each type of claim
🔹 Bodily injury & property damage claims
🔹 Medical expenses, lost wages & rehab coverage
🔹 Why most businesses need both policies in place
🔹 The simplest way to understand the difference between GL & WC

The easiest way to think about it:

General Liability = injuries or damage involving OTHER people

Workers Comp = injuries to YOUR employees while they’re working

If you own a business, understanding the difference between these two coverages is extremely important.

Um workers' comp, the there um when I was first getting started in the business and I was taking my first class, people would always say or the instructor would always say, "Workers' comp is king." So, if there's ever any doubt of coverage and an employee was injured, workers' comp is almost always going to be the policy that is involved and responds. Uh here in Michigan, it's on a no-fault basis, meaning that you don't necessarily have to prove if there was negligence or anything like that to get workers' comp to have a claim covered. Every business here in Michigan, if you have a full-time employee, you're going to be required to have workers' comp to be in compliance with the state. I believe every state has workers' comp insurance requirements besides Texas. I could be wrong, but I'm almost positive. Again, there really is not overlap between general liability insurance and workers' comp cuz general liability insurance is going to be related to, again, third parties, claims involving third parties. Workers' comp, and think internally, employees that get injured on the job. Those are the basics. Most times your business is going to need both. Construction cleaning is a legitimate trade and starting it the wrong way will cost you time, money, and credibility.

In this video, I break down how to start a construction cleaning company based on real field experience, not theory. We cover what most people overlook and how to approach construction cleaning like a professional operation.

This video is for:
• Anyone looking to start a construction cleaning business
• Existing cleaners who want to move into construction work
• Contractors who want to understand how professional cleaning fits into jobsite execution

I also put together a FREE construction cleaning startup checklist that walks through the fundamentals step by step.

👉 Grab it here: https://www.themillionairepb.com/checklist

If you’re serious about construction cleaning as a business not a side hustle, this video will save you from common mistakes.

👇 Drop questions in the comments. I read them.

#ConstructionCleaning
#CleaningBusiness
#StartACleaningBusiness
#ConstructionBusiness
#CommercialCleaning
#Entrepreneurship
#TradeBusiness

cleaned schools, restaurants, commercial

buildings. Construction cleaning changed

50 mile radius where construction is

clean. These are three different

your biggest weapon. It keeps you

underpricing jobs, not walking the first

based on dust level, debris level,

**Government Cleaning Contracts: How to Bid and Grow Your Cleaning Business**

Government cleaning and janitorial contracts can provide opportunities for cleaning businesses looking to expand their customer base and build long-term revenue.

But how do you find these contracts, understand the bidding requirements, and prepare your business to compete?

In this video, we explore government cleaning contract opportunities, the bidding process, and important considerations for small cleaning companies.

- Finding government cleaning and janitorial contracts
- Understanding bidding requirements
- Preparing a competitive proposal
- Evaluating staffing, equipment, and operating costs
- Planning for payroll and cash flow before payments arrive

At Owlsfield Financial Corporation, we help business owners explore financing options that fit their operations and cash flow.

This video breaks down the fundamentals of government procurement in a clear, engaging, and surprisingly entertaining way.

You’ll learn:
✅ What government contracting actually is

segments.text: ﻿What if I told you the biggest customer in the world is actively looking for new
businesses to buy from… and most people don’t
even realize they can compete? And no this customer isn’t Amazon.
It isn’t a Fortune 500 giant. It’s the U.S. government.
You don’t need secret connections. You don’t need to be a billion-dollar company.
And you definitely don’t need someone on the inside.
Because the government buys everything from everyday supplies all the way up to cutting-edge
tech and major construction projects. And the businesses that understand
how this system works? They’re the ones winning
the big opportunities. So let’s break it all down.
SECTION 1: What Government Contracting Actually Is
Government contracting is how federal, state, and local agencies purchase the
goods and services they need to operate. And trust me—the shopping list is wild.

This video detail a formal request for proposals issued by the City and County of San Francisco for janitorial services across several municipal buildings. The solicitation outlines specific administrative requirements, including the submission of pricing bids, written project strategies, and legal disclosures regarding past performance. A significant portion of the materials focuses on mandatory compliance with the Local Business Enterprise program, which provides incentives for certified small and local firms. Proposers are evaluated on a structured rating scale that assesses their management approach, environmental sustainability plans, and technical expertise. Additionally, the sources provide essential contractual terms, privacy policies, and deadline information managed through the Office of Contract Administration. Specialized forms for recycling compliance, hazardous waste handling, and labor relations history are also required for a complete submission.

In this episode, we’ll be discussing a high-level overview of our comprehensive 90-day property takeover checklist and how you can apply it to your next real estate closing. Whether you're a seasoned investor with multiple properties under your belt or a first-time buyer embarking on your real estate journey, this checklist will ensure you are well-prepared as you navigate the initial months of acquiring your new real estate space. So, sit back, grab a pen and paper, and get ready to dive into the world of strategic real estate property onboarding!

To join our investor community and stay updated on future opportunities, visit therequitygroup.com

Keynotes:

00:00:00 – Introduction
00:00:50 – What is the 90-day Property Onboarding plan?
00:01:27 –Setting up documents, banks, and credit lines
00:03:14 – Setting up your point of sale and accounting software
00:04:20 – Interviewing & hiring and collecting vendors
00:06:25 – Booking your travel
00:09:26 — Site setup
00:10:30 —Market/Comp Study
00:12:31 – Marketing and Branding setup
00:19:26 – Outro


Follow us on social media!

Dylan Marma https://www.linkedin.com/in/dylanmarma/
Luis Velez https://www.linkedin.com/in/luisevelez/
The Requity Group https://www.linkedin.com/company/requitygroup
Watch this podcast on YouTube https://www.youtube.com/@requity
Interested in becoming an investor? Visit https://www.therequitygroup.com to learn more.

#RVparkinvesting #propertymanagement #propertyonboarding #privateequity #realestate #investing

sites that you have on the property these are all the questions you want to be asking yourself when you're determining your site types usually you're then going to go ahead and create a really big campground map which is crucial because it makes it really easy for the guests to be able to navigate and understand which sites are where and when they're showing up for their check-ins it makes it easier for them to find their spot makes it a much more seamless process and when they're going through the booking map they're able to see what types of sites that they're going to be receiving along the way and then it's also important on your map to be able to emphasize all the key amenities so that if they're interested in Booking near a certain amenity or a certain site they can always look into being where they want to be throughout the campground next you have your Market study and Capital Improvements so hopefully early on in your due diligence you've done a thorough Market study but we don't think this is a one-time thing we think this is an iterative process so making sure that you're completing a thorough comp study and driving the comps getting a feel for what your local competitors look like and even building relationships with them though we call them competitors it's really more about I think of them even more as just comparables and you know work together with them to get a better feel for who else is in the area because a lot of times you're all serving different audiences anyway and you can kind of figure out how you can best strategize to work together and you want to get a feel for what they're charging for different rates to make sure that you're you're staying within market and and keeping a good pulse on any of the Ebbs and flows that may take place within that market then you're gonna go ahead and create a you should by now you should have especially before property onboarding you should have Capital Improvements about creating a Capital Improvements plan and really starting to make sure you have all the quotes in place for a lot of your capex budget so that you can begin to go out there and execute for us we're really big on lining up what we call Early impact projects so we want to be thinking about what are the things that we need to do to bring this place to its highest potential and that could be amenities right what amenities are you bringing into the campground are you upgrading sites sometimes you might upgrade partial hookup sites to full hookup sites or 30 amp electric to 50 amp electric are you going to renovate the clubhouse are you going to hold more events right know what your early impact projects are and communicate them right once you once you once they're set in stone and you feel confident you're going to go you're going to be able to execute on these projects you have in mind communicating those can be a really helpful way to sort of win win over the the guests from the place and and you know get their buy-in that you really are here to make this a better place and it's not going downhill as a lot of them might fear when they see a new ownership in town right they want to they want to get comfortable with you and the best way you can do it is to tell them what you're going to do and then follow through on your word and show them that you know you do what you say you're going to do next up we have marketing and branding so getting your online presence right is crucial generally we recommend before property onboarding that you start you have a website set up if you're going to Rebrand the website or whatever it might be you know getting your online presence established getting the site up and running and linking that to the previous domain if you are switching domains so that you don't lose the traction that the domain has when it comes to the SEO you want to order new signage so in addition to now you might have new logos and signage ordering signage with your sign providers for your on-site real estate creating brochures marketing flyers and welcome packets that you can hand out on site and then again back online you have your Google ads Facebook ads and you might also be doing some physical Billboards as well making sure you have your ad set up and you know day one you're ready to start getting the word out there as much as possible about you know the the improvements you plan to make and and that sort of thing and Facebook groups Facebook pages are really really important as well so it's all about you know again communication exciting the right expectations and following through on those expectations is the number one way to be able to get the you know the buy-in and build the community that you're hoping to build from there you have make sure you're double checking all of your inventory and accounts so we've mentioned creating your inventory list and making sure you go through the store and see what they currently have in inventory and then and then make sure you have a clear list of what you plan to order and keeping track of your inventory that also doubles to your two-year maintenance inventory right you might have certain things that you keep on on Deck when it comes to maybe it's your you know your Linens and your towels and your your soap for your short-term rentals or maybe it's things like you may have a on-site storage and a bunch of tools that the that the maintenance team uses and make sure you have an inventory of what tools are on property so nothing just goes missing when you're able to keep a good pulse and and keep be proactive with you know order your inventory management side of things then you have your transfer and setting up of new accounts with vendors so you want to make sure that you know before property closes that you're in touch with the water and sewer company the Wi-Fi company the propane company if you have cable the cable company the trash company maybe Landscaping you know all of the vendors that are you know making the day-to-day run you want to be working with them and ensuring that you're there to either transfer over the account or set up a new account with them so day one you're not scrambling or you're not having the you know the power company come out and turn your lights off or anything like that so then from there we're going to be engaging we generally do a cost segregation study to be able to help maximize the tax advantages for the community so we usually around the time of closing we'll engage our cost segregation expert to go out and begin to help us understand the useful life of each aspect of the campground so that at the end of the year when it comes to tax time we are able to maximize the the tax advantages now communication I've already stressed this a lot but it's really important to communicate well and early with with your people people just don't like change and it makes them uncomfortable so I think it's really important that you have a takeover or I like to even say just an onboarding notice you know the of the transfer of ownership that's taking place so that the current residents or guests you're able to you know deliver to them the news of any and really clearly outline any changes that are taking place if there is changes in the rates that's going to be a big question so we usually recommend just getting ahead of that and being clear on what the updated rate schedule is going to look like if there is changes in you know amenities or the way things are going to be run be clear and proactive on that and and hopefully you know our objective is always to have the good news outweigh any bad news in these communications you know if there is rate increases that are taking place we want to be able collaborative work collaboratively with with the guests from our different communities and we we don't have a hard set in stone capex plan for every dollar before we close on the property we like to actually get a feel for what the people want and kind of survey the the different guests or residents and get a sense of what do they want what are what's in high demand there who are they and how can you're setting up your Google my business we're all about you know Google reviews and Google my business takes usually a few days to kind of get up and running so get your claim your Facebook page claim your Google my business if making sure you're talking with the current ownership group ahead of time if they're if they have existing ones to make sure that transition goes smoothly and then you know really make sure you're spending the proper time to train the new team members effectively so that's all for today's episode that's just a high level overview of our takeover checklist and I'm metadata.title: Getting Your Cleaning Company from $500K- $1M vs.  $1M- $5M
metadata.author: Grow My Cleaning Company
metadata.shortDescription:
What gets you to $500K–$1M  is not always what gets you to $1M–$5M. 
Luke built his commercial cleaning company to $1M/ year while serving as a full-time pastor and asks Mike what needs to change to get to $5M/ year while maintaining his freedom. 

Discover what cleaning company culture looks like  at different stages & revenue levels?

If you’re stuck at the same revenue level and would like some help, shoot Mike an email at mike@growmycleaningcompany.com- he personally answers every one!

metadata.title: How I Built a $1M Airbnb Cleaning Business — Without Cleaning a Single Unit
metadata.author: Logan Robison
metadata.shortDescription:
I started my Airbnb cleaning business in late 2022. We just crossed $1,000,000 in lifetime sales — and I haven't personally cleaned a unit in years. Here's exactly how I did it (and how you can too).

---

In this FREE 2-hour masterclass with Home Service Academy, I break down the complete roadmap to starting and growing a profitable Airbnb cleaning business — even if you're currently cleaning yourself and want to stop.

**What You'll Learn:**
- Why Airbnb cleaning is one of the best low-overhead service businesses you can start right now
- How to land your first short-term rental clients (even with zero reviews or references)
- The exact systems I used to hire and manage cleaners so I could step off the mop
- How to price your services to be profitable from day one
- How to scale past $10K/month and build a team that runs without you
- The mindset shift that separates cleaners from business owners

**This masterclass is for you if:**
✅ You're currently cleaning Airbnbs and want to make more money
✅ You want to start an Airbnb cleaning business but don't know where to begin
✅ You're tired of trading time for money and want to build something that scales
✅ You want a real business — not just a side hustle

**About Logan:**
I launched my cleaning company in late 2022 and grew it to over $1,000,000 in lifetime sales by building systems, hiring great cleaners, and focusing on short-term rental clients. I now help other cleaners do the same.

🔗 Ready to start? Get free training at: join.samedayturn.com
Webinar hosted by @homeserviceacademy1314

metadata.title: Starting a $120K/Month Cleaning Business From Scratch
metadata.author: UpFlip
metadata.shortDescription:
How much can you make with a house cleaning business? Queen Bee Cleaning Service is poised to bring in $1.5 million in revenue in 2021—a big jump from the $5,000 the cleaning company started with in 2015. If you’re curious what they did to grow so quickly, you’ll want to watch this interview. 

Cristobal Mondragon wasn’t sure about starting a cleaning business when his wife posed the idea. Three months after Queen Bee Cleaning Service opened, she was bringing home a bigger paycheck than him—and Cristobal quit his job and went all-in on their cleaning service business. We’ll hear their strategy for growing revenue quickly, and how they maximized a small start-up budget to get them off to a running start.  

Not knowing how to start a cleaning business before you jump in can lead to costly mistakes. We’ll find out what missteps Queen Bee’s owners made early on, what problems those caused, and how they recovered. They’ll also share what systems and processes a cleaning business start up needs to hire staff and build a team that provides a consistently exceptional customer experience. 

A cleaning business can’t succeed without customers. We’ll learn Queen Bee’s tips and strategies for marketing their business, and what Cristobal learned from his previous career in online marketing that helped his cleaning company build their customer base. 

Watch a 2nd interview we've done with Chris: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YcYIYdqegGA

(upbeat music) - Today, how many employees do you have? What do you pay them and how do you retain them to stay with you and? - Yes, yes. Good question. So as of now we have 22 cleaners. They all range from $19 per hour. You know, the people who doesn't drive. - [Paul] Okay. - [Chris] The drivers get 20 to 22. If they're driving my car it's $20. If they drive their car is 24. It's a step-by-step process that works for any service business owner. metadata.author: SEO Growth Partners
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Joey from SEO Growth Partners Digital Marketing breaks down how we helped NextGen Cleaning, a commercial cleaning and janitorial services company in Portland, Oregon, generate consistent qualified leads through SEO, GEO, Google Business Profile optimization, AI search visibility, Google Ads, and website strategy.

NextGen Cleaning was a newer business when we started working together. They did not have years of built-up SEO authority, a massive brand, or a huge online lead pipeline.

They were building from the ground up.

In this video, I walk through real lead examples from the past 45 days and show the qualified form submissions coming through their website. Names and personal details are hidden, but the lead quality is clear.

Over that recent 45-day period, they generated roughly 9 to 10 qualified form leads. On top of that, the client has told us they average about 4 to 5 qualified inbound phone leads per month from people who call directly instead of submitting a form.

That means NextGen Cleaning is averaging 10+ qualified leads per month from online search.

For a commercial cleaning company, that is extremely meaningful because many of these leads can turn into recurring revenue.

A single weekly office cleaning account could be worth $250 per week, which is more than $1,000 per month in recurring revenue. Other leads may be for one-time projects like post-construction cleaning, move-out cleaning, floor cleaning, or commercial cleanouts.

So while 10 qualified leads per month might not sound massive on the surface, the business impact can be huge.

Based on what the client has shared with us, they are bringing in an estimated $3,000+ per month in recurring revenue from online-generated leads, plus additional revenue from one-time commercial cleaning jobs and post-construction cleanups.

Over the past 12 months, they have told us they have added roughly $25,000 to $30,000 per month in monthly recurring revenue.

That is the power of SEO and Google Ads when they are tied to real commercial intent.

For commercial cleaning companies and janitorial service providers, people do not all search the same way.

Some search broadly:

Commercial cleaning company Portland
Commercial cleaning services near me
Janitorial services Portland
Janitorial company near me
Office cleaning company Portland

Others search more specifically:

Commercial post-construction cleaning Portland
Commercial floor cleaning company
Office cleaning services Beaverton
Janitorial services Hillsboro
Commercial cleaning company Lake Oswego
Weekly office cleaning services
Move-out cleaning for commercial space
Restaurant cleaning company
Medical office cleaning services
Warehouse cleaning services

That is why the strategy cannot just be one generic homepage that says, “We offer cleaning services.”

The website needs to clearly explain:

What services they offer
Where they provide those services
Who they help
How the process works
What types of commercial spaces they clean
Why someone should trust them
How to request a quote

For NextGen Cleaning, we built a strategy around exactly that.

We created content and landing pages targeting both broad and specific commercial cleaning searches.

That included pages for:

Commercial cleaning services
Janitorial services
Commercial post-construction cleaning
Commercial floor cleaning
Office cleaning
Service area pages
Beaverton commercial cleaning
Hillsboro commercial cleaning
Lake Oswego commercial cleaning
Portland-area commercial cleaning

This matters because Google, Google Maps, ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and prospective customers all need clear information to understand when a company is relevant.

A business owner or property manager searching for commercial post-construction cleaning should not land on a vague cleaning page that barely mentions construction cleanup.

Someone searching for commercial floor cleaning should land on a page that clearly explains floor cleaning services.

Someone searching for janitorial services in Beaverton should land on content that makes it obvious the company serves Beaverton.

That is the foundation of modern commercial cleaning SEO, janitorial services SEO, GEO, GBO, and AI search visibility.

In this video, we cover:

How NextGen Cleaning grew qualified online leads as a newer commercial cleaning company
Why commercial cleaning SEO needs both service pages and location pages
How janitorial services companies can generate recurring revenue from search
Why qualified leads matter more than traffic
How recurring commercial cleaning accounts change the ROI equation
Why post-construction cleaning pages can attract high-intent leads
Why commercial floor cleaning pages can drive better search visibility
How service area pages help local businesses rank in nearby cities
How Google Business Profile optimization supports local cleaning leads
How AI search and GEO are changing local service marketing

metadata.title: How to Start a Commercial Cleaning Business for $4,200
metadata.author: Business From Zero
metadata.shortDescription:
Commercial cleaning business startup costs in 2026 prove you do not need to risk an $80,000 franchise fee or sign a commercial loan at 7.5% interest to replace a $75,000 W-2 paycheck. While the median American household holds just $8,000 in liquid savings, recurring B2B commercial janitorial lets you operate after 6:00 PM for $4,200 out of pocket—without quitting your 9-to-5.

In this financial audit, we break down the exact startup CapEx, per-building unit economics, monthly operating expenses (OpEx), and a real monthly P&L showing how 5 commercial contracts generate $6,100/month in pre-tax net cash flow. We also expose the three hidden traps that cause 64% of beginners to go broke in Year 1.

Complete Financial Ledger Summary (5 Recurring B2B Accounts):
• Total Startup CapEx: $4,200 (Section 179 tax-deductible in Year 1)
• Monthly Gross Inflow (5 Accounts @ $1,800/mo avg): $9,000
• Monthly Operating Expenses (OpEx): $2,900
• Pre-Tax Net In-Hand Cash Flow: $6,100 / month (67.7% Net Operating Margin)
• Payback Period: Under 3 Weeks (at full 5-account route stabilization)

Timestamps:
0:00 - The $4,200 Commercial Cleaning Reality vs. The $80K Franchise Trap
0:24 - Target Profit ($6,100/Mo) & How Recurring B2B Contracts Work
1:04 - Setup CapEx ($4,200) & Trap #1: Overcapitalizing & Missing $2M Bonding
2:59 - Unit Economics ($1,800 Dental Clinic) & Trap #2: IRS 1099 Penalties
4:58 - Landing 5 Accounts (Walkthrough Script) & Trap #3: Net-30 Cash Crunches
6:39 - Consolidated Monthly P&L Ledger ($9,000 Gross vs. $2,900 OpEx)
8:40 - US Automation Tech Stack (Swept, QuickBooks, Gusto, OpenPhone)
9:43 - The Scaling Flywheel ($11,000+/Mo Semi-Absentee)

Key Takeaways from This Audit:
• Commercial vs. Residential: Work after 6:00 PM on auto-renewing B2B annual contracts instead of chasing one-off $120 residential jobs during working hours.
• Pricing Strategy: Bid based on restroom fixture count ($45–$55/billable labor hour) rather than rough square footage alone.
• Compliance: Avoid IRS 1099 misclassification penalties by structuring recurring night cleaners as part-time W-2 employees and carrying a $10,000 Janitorial Surety Bond.

👇 Want the exact Square-Footage Bidding Calculator & P&L Spreadsheet used in this video? Comment "LEDGER" below!

Subscribe to Business From Zero for weekly, unvarnished financial audits of real American businesses.

Disclaimer: All financial figures, labor classifications (part-time W-2 vs. 1099 independent contractor), tax references (Section 179 deductions and FICA/self-employment taxes), and insurance estimates in this video are for educational modeling purposes only and do not constitute legal, CPA, or employment law advice. Always consult a licensed CPA, business attorney, and commercial insurance broker in your state before hiring workers or signing commercial service agreements.

Classify recurring crew as part-time W-2 employees at $18 an hour plus a 12% employer FICA and workers comp burden costing $377 a month per staffed building. On a single staffed $1,800 account, after $377 in W-2 labor and $135 in wholesale supplies and fuel, you keep $1,288 in gross unit contribution. Pause card two here to verify the per building unit math. Quick question for you. If you had $4,200 in savings today, would you clean your first three accounts solo at night to pocket 100% of the labor or hire part-time night staff from day one? Comment solo or hire below. I read every single reply. Signing your first five commercial buildings does not require paying $400 a month to Yelp or Thumbtack, which brings us directly to trap number three. Lead aggregator burn and net 30 invoice cash crunches. Beginners waste thousands buying shared leads on residential apps where five competitors race to the bottom on price. Instead, put on a clean branded polo shirt, grab a clipboard, and walk into suburban class B medical plazas, outpatient clinics, and multi-tenant office parks between 10:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m. Never pitch like a desperate salesperson. Say this word for word to the office manager. Hi, I'm with Apex Commercial Care. We service three medical suites down on Oak Street and we're doing walkthroughs in this plaza today because we have capacity for one more evening account on our Tuesday, Thursday, and Sunday route. Who handles your current janitorial vendor review if you ever need a backup quote? Once you win the walkthrough and send your proposal, watch out for the second half of trap number three, corporate net 30 payment delays. Medical groups and property management firms typically pay 30 days after you submit your monthly invoice. Protect your cash flow by writing a mandatory first month retainer upfront into your service agreement and always add a 15% markup when restocking the client's toilet paper, paper towels, and hand soap. Now let's consolidate the entire operation into a realistic monthly P&L ledger once you stabilize five commercial accounts averaging $1,800 each. That puts your monthly gross inflow at exactly $9,000. In this realistic hybrid model, you personally clean two buildings on weeknights, about 10 hours a week, and staff the other three buildings with part-time W-2 night cleaners. Here is every dollar leaving your business checking account every 30 days. Part-time W-2 crew payroll and employer FICA taxes across three accounts, $1,130. Monthly commercial general liability, surety bond, and workers' comp insurance, $245. Wholesale commercial disinfectants, trash liners, and restock consumables, $380. Vehicle fuel and commercial auto policy rider, $290. Scheduling software, QuickBooks Online, and Open Phone business line, $135. Local B2B postcard mailers and Google Business Profile ads, $420. Equipment maintenance and contingency reserve, $300. Total monthly OPEX equals $2,900. Subtract $2,900 in expenses from $9,000 in recurring B2B retainers, and you clear $6,100 per month in pre-tax net cash flow, a 67.7% net operating margin. Even after setting aside 25% for federal income and self-employment taxes, your initial $4,200 CAPEX pays itself back in under 3 weeks of full route operation. Pause card three right now to inspect the complete monthly P&L ledger. To manage five commercial buildings from your smartphone without missing a single shift while working your W-2 job, install four core US automation tools from week one. First, use Swept or Connect Team for GPS geofenced clock-ins, which sends an instant alert to your phone if a night cleaner has not arrived at a clinic by 6:15 p.m., alongside mandatory before and after photo checklists. Second, run QuickBooks Online to automate recurring net 30 ACH invoices so corporate clients pay via bank transfer with 0 2.9% credit card processing fees. Third, put your part-time crew on Gusto so direct deposits, W-2 tax withholdings, and workers' comp filings run on autopilot. Fourth, use OpenPhone for a dedicated local business line with automated missed call text follow-ups. Once your first five accounts generate $6,100 a month in net cash flow, you trigger the scaling flywheel. Reinvest just two months of net profits, roughly $12,000, to hire a full-time W-2 evening route supervisor to take over your final two buildings and scale the 12 commercial accounts. At 12 doors, your net cash flow crosses $11,000 a month completely semi-absentee, giving you the debt-free capital to exit your W-2 job and acquire cash-flowing physical real estate. metadata.title: Commercial Cleaning: How to Win Your First Office Contract (Walkthrough + Bid Worksheet)
metadata.author: Solo Business Systems
metadata.shortDescription:
Your best residential client is worth about $400 a month — and they can cancel with a text. One ordinary office contract is worth $1,000 a month, $12,000 a year, signed for twelve months. But you can't win it the residential way: no phone price, no handshake. Commercial cleaning runs on credentials, walkthroughs, and written bids — and in this video I hand you the two documents that win these contracts: a nine-point walkthrough checklist and a five-line bid worksheet, worked end-to-end on one benchmark office (5,000 sq ft, 3 nights a week) until it prices out at exactly $1,000 a month. Screenshot both documents when they appear — they're the whole system.

In this video:
- What actually changes when you cross from residential to commercial cleaning
- The credential gate: the $1M/$2M liability, COI, $25K janitorial bond and workers' comp proof clients ask for before they hand you a key
- Where the first office contracts actually come from (and the one question that opens the walkthrough)
- The nine-point walkthrough checklist that births an accurate price
- The five-line bid worksheet: time, labour, supplies, overhead, margin — $650 + $50 + $100 = $800 cost, +25% = $1,000/month
- The per-square-foot trap: why the internet's 5–20 cents math ($250–$1,000 a visit) loses to signed reality ($700–$2,800 a month)
- The service agreement clauses that protect the margin, including the added-space re-price
- Net-30 reality: the day-60 first payment, and the two defences for the cash gap
- The five commercial mistakes every residential convert makes

metadata.title: How to Clean Up Bloodborne Pathogens: A Methodical Guide to Safety and Compliance
metadata.author: Imperial Brady
metadata.shortDescription:
It’s estimated that approximately three million exposures to bloodborne pathogens, or BBPs, occur annually, largely in healthcare settings and from accidental punctures.

The Occupational Health and Safety Administration, or OSHA, defines BBPs as “infectious microorganisms in human blood that can cause disease in humans.” As such, it should come as no surprise that it’s absolutely critical to properly handle and clean up bodily fluid spills to prevent the possible spread of any BBPs or OPIMs. 

OPIMs, which stands for other potentially infectious materials, is a broader term used to encompass other potentially infectious bodily fluids, such as vomit or diarrhea, that are also common outside of the healthcare industry. 

While we’ll continue to use the term BBP for this video, understand that what we’re saying applies to OPIMs all the same. 

OSHA has a set of standards and regulations for handling BBPs and OPIMs. To stay compliant with the OSHA standards, business professionals are required to undergo annual training. 

This video provides a detailed walkthrough of cleanup procedures, highlighting the use of proper disinfectants and personal protective equipment, or PPE, to prioritize safety and compliance.

While the BBP cleanup protocol may vary slightly from facility to facility, it should always be centered around these seven steps: cleanup prep, initial cleanup, deep clean, disposal and disinfection, PPE removal, waste management, and record and report. 

The first step is to gather supplies and prioritize personal safety.
best. 

Step two is to commence the cleanup process.

Step three is to perform a deep clean and disinfection.

Step four is to dispose of the bodily fluid spill material safely.

Step five is to remove PPE safely. 

Step six revolves around waste management. 

Step seven is to record and report the incident. 

Cleaning Vs Disinfecting: https://www.imperialdade.com/blog/cleaning-vs-sanitizing-vs-disinfecting

Bloodborne Pathogens Training: https://www.imperialdade.com/cleaning-institute
