metadata.shortDescription:
This OSHA bloodborne pathogens course is a preview to a comprehensive training program designed to educate individuals on the prevention and management of exposure to bloodborne pathogens in the workplace. 


You can find the full course here: 
joseph-cox-s-school1.teachable.com/p/bloodborne-pathogens-training-osha

Certificate upon completion of quiz. This course trainer is certified by OSHA through bloodbornetraining.com



Stay OSHA Compliant


The bloodborne pathogen training program has been developed to satisfy all requirements nationwide. We help you maintain compliance while ensuring the highest quality training material available.

This course covers essential topics such as identifying potential sources of bloodborne pathogens like HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C, understanding transmission methods, and implementing effective exposure control plans. Participants learn best practices for using personal protective equipment (PPE), handling and disposing of contaminated materials, and responding to exposure incidents to reduce the risk of infection. By completing an OSHA-compliant course, individuals and organizations ensure that they meet federal safety standards, fostering a safer working environment and empowering employees with knowledge that protects both themselves and others.

metadata.title: Case Study: Misclassification of Employees as Independent Contractors
metadata.author: BICO Legal and Compliance Consulting, LLC
metadata.shortDescription: Case Study: Misclassification of Employees as Independent Contractors

segments.text: I'm currently advising a client who is a
licensed barber in the State of Florida
who has been misclassified as a 1099
independent contractor my client and the
owner of the hair salon where she worked
executed an independent contract
agreement however my client had no
ability to negotiate her agreement the
terms were set by the salon owner and
offered to my client on a take it or
leave a basis moreover the terms of the
independent contractor agreement as they
were applied to my client did not
reflect the true working conditions
policies or pay practices at the salon
during my client's tenure at the salon
she was under the direction and control
of the salon owners and therefore was
treated as an employee not an
independent contractor for example the
salon owners directly dictated how my
client charged customers inside the
salon my client did not have the
autonomy to set her own prices and to
determine her pricing structure the
salon owners used the threat of
dismissal or termination to exercise
control over my client and to force her
to comply with the salon's pricing
policy the salon owners required my
client to maintain a set of a set
schedule between 10:00 a.m. and 500m
whether or not customers needed to be
served the salon owners expected my
client to remain loyal to the salon and
my client reasonbly believed that she
was not free to work wherever she
pleased including for competing
businesses without the risk that
defendants would terminate their
employment relationship with her the
salon owners required my client to
devote a full-time work schedule to the
salon and therefore restricted my client
from doing other gainful work the salon
owners willfully violated the fair labor
standards act by failing to pay my
client minimum wage for all the hours
worked during her tenure at the salon as
my client in fact was treated as an
employee
she occupied a non-exempt position with
the salon and was entitled to receive at
least the minimum wage in overtime pay
what should you do if you believe that
you've been misclassified as a 1099
independent contractor first talk to
your employer have a conversation with
your manager or H or the HR department
uh
executive clearly outlining your
concerns about being misclassified as an
independent contractor and explain why
you believe you should be considered as
an employee based on your work
responsibilities and level of control
second gather evidence keep detailed
records of your work activities
Communications with your employer and
any documentation that demonstrates your
level of supervision and dependence on
the company thirdly request a formal
review ask your employer to formally
review your classification and provide a
written explanation for their decision
if they maintain your independent cont
contractor status and finally consult
with an employment lawyer if your
employer is unwilling to address your
concerns seek legal advice from an
employment attorney who can assess your
situation and advise on the best course
of action

metadata.title: Everything You Need to Know Before Setting Up Your Own Janitorial Franchise
metadata.author: Grow My Cleaning Company
metadata.shortDescription:
In today's episode, Mike shares his wisdom on franchising a business with Cleaning Nation and Cynthia, owner of Janco Janitorial http://jancojanitorial.net/ 

There are a couple of ways to franchise your business. The first step is to decide which model best suits your needs/desire first.

Standard Franchise Model

In this model, a Franchisee would give you a sum of money up front for your janitorial franchise. In exchange, you give them operations manuals, training, use of your trademark and support. 

After that initial investment they would give between 5-10% of their revenue per month in perpetuity. 

RESOURCE ALERT: Check out our episode with David Luke, owner of Two Maids and a Mop http://www.growmycleaningcompany.com/cleaning-company-franchise/

Cleaning Industry Variation Model

Here, you would take a much smaller upfront fee and dole out small cleaning accounts to your franchisees. As the franchisor, you would keep 20% and they would keep 80%. You would be responsible for marketing, billing, customer support and finding jobs.  Your franchisees would handle the cleaning and everything related to performing the work. 

RESOURCE ALERT: To learn more about this model check out this episode with Stephen Coade http://www.growmycleaningcompany.com/cleaning-franchise/

For both models however, getting started isn't as simple as "Give me money and I will lend you my name and handbook". 

Franchising has a pretty well regulated legal structure. 

The process of setting up a janitorial franchise is actually pretty involved and may not be financially worth while for only 1 franchisee. You want to start with an agency that all they do is set up franchises. They will help you walk through the legal paperwork to become qualified as a franchisor. It's safe to assume that paperwork may cost you upwards of $30-$50,000.

KEY POINT: Calculate the start up cost before moving forward

Next, there's the systems part. You are going to be taking a lot of money from someone up front. You want to be able to look them in the eye and say " I have done this, I have repeated it and as long as you do what I am going to tell you to do, you will be successful."

In order to be able to do that, first open 2-3 company owned stores. Put them in different areas and go through the process of getting them up and running successfully. Document what you do and the systems you use thoroughly. You could even have your first "franchisee" manage one of your satellite locations.

RESOURCE ALERT: Go to http://www.growmycleaningcompany.com/creating-systems-for-growth/ to learn more about creating systems

But, if you have a ton of money and are totally in to starting a legitimate franchise there are some other considerations to make. Just like when you move from cleaning to running a business, you learn it's a totally different set of skills. Owning a cleaning business is very different than selling a janitorial franchise.

A franchisor's job is to attract clients, create systems and always be on top of giving the tools to the franchisees. It's your responsibility to make sure you do everything you can to help your franchisees have success. If you aren't confident you can deliver, then you have no business taking anyone's money for a janitorial franchise!

Too often what happens is you will cut corners or to make money or you'll raise prices to what you think is appropriate and never win bids and blame everyone for that or just quit. It's important that you understand that business is what you chose and the trade is cleaning. You must be good at business to demand a profit. Our job as business owners is to control our expenses as much as possible, so we can be competitive and make our margins. Whining about not making enough money is a you problem if you are not controlling costs, training your employees, supervising your jobs, and reducing workplace injuries. Bidding jobs should be the easy part. Running a business truly is the hard part. I also want to add a little disclaimer here that your business expenses will fluctuate and change as you grow. The smaller you are, the less your actual expenses will be because you're performing the majority of the duties that we discussed. As you grow, you can't do it all yourself, so you have to outsource, hire, or both. That means that your expenses are going to rise, and if you price jobs at the I do it myself rate, you're going to immediately lose money when you start to scale. I have seen this hundreds of times. Heck, I have lived it. Plan ahead and recognize the possible costs associated with performing these duties now and as you grow. When you do this, you will bid jobs correctly now and will still have profit when you start to scale. You may also wonder how large organizations can bid so low when you can't. Well, they control their costs and have hit a critical mass with their overhead expenses. They can take more and more business on with the same predictable expense for overhead. We all strive for this reality, but for now, plan ahead and complete your calculations. As promised, this would be a full video on how to get your numbers right. Now it's up to you to make it happen. Check out the description of this video for the link to watch how to bid commercial cleaning jobs. If you're serious about growing your business, become a YouTube member today. For only $5 a month, you gain access to live videos where we discuss important topics in detail and answer questions from our viewers in real time. Thank you for watching, and we'll see you next time.

metadata.title: Keep it Clean Episode 047 Bloodborne Pathogen Training
metadata.author: Keep It Clean
metadata.shortDescription:
Bloodborne Pathogens Training

DOC’s Facilities offers online janitorial training for safety on Bloodborne pathogens. This training is frequently dismissed as non-critical for frontline cleaners. In our experience, this attitude is rarely a disregard for employee safety. It’s more often due to at least two situations that are common in the commercial cleaning industry:
1. Assuming that contacting blood will only happen in healthcare facilities
2. The simple economics of cleaning staff turnover

Let’s address these one at a time.
Assuming that contacting blood will only happen in healthcare facilities
Some of the most common situations for front line cleaners are basic office cleaning. These involve:
Dusting and cleaning table lamps
Cleaning Desks 
Cleaning Restrooms
General cleaning for Reception Areas 
Counter and tabletop Cleaning in Kitchenette & Breakrooms
Emptying trash

If none of that jumps out at you as a potential bloodborne pathogen risk, you’re not alone. The reality is that almost all of them COULD be. Now that is a little extreme. But the simple act of emptying trash cans exposes front line cleaners. Coughing and blowing your nose and throwing that tissue away places droplets into the trash. Mopping spit or vomit produces the same (but a more obvious) risk of exposure to bloodborne pathogens.

And then there’s the restroom. More specifically the feminine hygiene receptacles. 


The simple economics of cleaning staff turnover

The commercial cleaning industry can often feel like a “race-to-zero”. For less-informed customers, cleaning is seen as a necessary and low-level service. In client businesses where this attitude prevails, that means “get cleaning as cheap as you can”.

On average, cleaning staff turn-over can range from 75% - 300%. That means that many companies spend as little as possible to train their staff. The funds to train have to come from somewhere and few employers or clients accept the necessity until something negative happens.

Training Your Cleaners
Commercial cleaning company owners and those in Environmental services understand. We don’t expect most people to change their minds. The general assumption is that you don’t have to be “the brightest bulb” to be a cleaner. Regardless of our opinion on that, it is an industry where you can start with little education. And it’s also one where you can excel and have a tremendous, positive impact on hundreds of people when you gain knowledge and perform your tasks well.

Cleaning for Health
As a lead training organization for cleaning companies and employers with cleaning staff, our singular focus is “Cleaning for Health”. 

Most often this statement is interpreted as maintaining a clean environment for employees, customers and visitors entering a facility. However, we hold that this applies to cleaning & environmental staff, first. Your knowledge of safety practices for the proper use of PPE (Personal Protective Equipment), cleaning equipment and cleaning materials will set the bar for your ability to do the job well AND provide an excellent future for yourself in the environmental services industry.

All facilities where people are present have inherent risk of exposure. This training intends to help you mitigate the hazards of bloodborne pathogens. It’s designed with a testing & grading component. This is priced to meet the needs of companies and inside teams. This training can be used as a stand-alone or as a primer for full OSHA training. 

If you have questions on this bloodborne pathogen training or full staff training, please contact us online or by phone at 585-413-0574.

metadata.title: How Jani-King Makes Money — The $3,000 Mop Empire
metadata.author: Ledger & Ruin
metadata.shortDescription:
A night auditor borrowed $3,000 — and built the world's largest cleaning franchise. This is how Jani-King makes money: not by mopping floors, but by selling customers to the people who mop them.

Jim Cavanaugh was a night auditor at a Holiday Inn in Norman, Oklahoma, when he befriended the hotel's night janitor, Don McGuffin. McGuffin was too busy cleaning to find new customers — so Cavanaugh found them for him, for a finder's fee. In 1969 he borrowed $3,000 from a school friend and founded Jani-King. Five years later the company began franchising, with a twist no other franchise had: the regional office signs the cleaning contracts and hands them to the franchisee as initial business. The franchisee buys customers, not just a brand. This is the story of that trick — and the disclosure-document math behind it, from the $16,000–$57,000 cost of a unit franchise to the average unit's $118,000 in gross sales and the fee stack that turns thousands of small cuts into an $859 million system.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The $859 Million Mop Empire
0:41 Norman
2:42 Day and Night
4:50 The Franchise
7:05 The Money
9:31 The Empire
11:31 The Name

SOURCES

MSA Worldwide, "Franchisor Profile: Jerry Crawford, Jani-King": https://msaworldwide.com/franchisor-interviews-and-profiles/franchisor-profile-jerry-crawford-jani-king/

segments.text: Nine thousand franchisees.
More than sixty thousand customers.
And eight hundred fifty-nine million dollars in
system sales in a single year.
That is what a mop empire looks like today.
It started with a night auditor in Norman,
Oklahoma, who owned no cleaning company at all.
This video answers one question: how does
that man end up owning the
company that cleans the World Cup?
Three thousand dollars, borrowed from a school friend.
That is the ending in miniature.
But the real story is not the money.
It is a trick, and the
trick is in chapter three.
He never sold cleaning.
He sold customers.
And once you see the trick, you will see
it in every franchise you have ever walked past.
Jim Cavanaugh was a business student at the
University of Oklahoma, and to pay his way
he took the night shift at a Holiday
Inn in Norman: night auditor, the man who
balanced the books while the town slept.
The night auditor's job was numbers, not mops.
He checked guests in late, checked
the ledger, and waited for morning.
And every night, the same
man mopped past his desk.
That man was Don McGuffin, the hotel's night janitor.
He cleaned the same floors Cavanaugh walked, and the
two of them became friends in the small
hours, when nobody else was awake to talk.
McGuffin had a complaint, and it
was not about the pay.
He and his crew were so busy cleaning
at night that he had no time left
to look for new business during the day.
Think about that problem.
The work was there.
The customers were out there.
The only thing missing was the hours to go
and find them, because the nights were already full.
Cavanaugh saw what McGuffin could not.
A janitor's problem is a salesman's opportunity,
if someone else does the selling.
And the night auditor had empty
days and a head for numbers.
So he made McGuffin a deal.
Cavanaugh would find him new cleaning work,
and McGuffin would pay him a finder's
fee for every customer he brought in.
No mops.
No buckets.
Just introductions.
That deal is the whole story
in miniature, so remember it.
Cavanaugh did not start by cleaning a single floor.
He started by selling the customer to
the man who cleaned the floor.
The finder's fees came in,
one customer at a time.
It was small money, and it was slow money.
But it proved something no classroom had taught him:
the customer was worth more than the cleaning.
Here is the first payoff this video promised you.
His first sale was not a mop,
a bucket, or an hour of scrubbing.
It was a name, an address, and a
signed cleaning contract, handed to another man.
That shape — find the customer, hand
over the work, keep a cut
— would become a billion-dollar machine.
But first, Cavanaugh had to learn the other
half of the business: the cleaning itself.
In nineteen sixty-eight, a year before the company
existed, Cavanaugh was already living two lives.
By day he marketed janitorial services around Norman.
By night he serviced the clients himself.
Days selling, nights cleaning.
He was his own first employee, his own
first customer, and his own first lesson in
what the work actually cost in sweat.
He was not pretending to be a cleaner.
He was learning the trade from the floor
up, so that when he sold a contract
he knew exactly what he was promising.
But two lives do not scale.
One man can only clean so many
floors in a night, and every
new customer made the nights longer.
He needed money, and he needed
help, and he had neither.
The money came first.
In nineteen sixty-nine, Cavanaugh borrowed three thousand dollars
from a school friend and founded Jani-King.
Three thousand dollars, a borrowed
stake, and a borrowed idea.
Three thousand dollars is not much.
It would not buy a truck,
a crew, or an office.
What it bought was time: time to sell
during the day without starving at night.
He dropped out of university to do it.
The degree could wait.
The idea could not, because every month
he stayed in class was a
month someone else could steal it.
That same year, nineteen sixty-nine, he opened
his first full-time office in Norman, Oklahoma.
One room, one phone, and a list
of customers he had found himself.
Notice the constraint ladder here, because
it runs the whole story.
No money, so he borrowed it.
No crew, so he did the cleaning himself.
No customers, so he went and found them.
Each constraint had the same answer: do
the missing piece yourself until you can
pay someone else to do it.
The problem was the next constraint,
and it was the biggest one.
One office in Norman could only clean Norman.
To grow, he needed cleaners in every town,
and he could not hire them all himself.
The answer was not hiring.
It was franchising.
But franchising a cleaning company was
a strange idea in nineteen sixty-nine.
Nobody franchised mops.
Which is exactly why it worked — and
the next chapter is the trick itself.
In nineteen seventy-four, five years after the first office,
Jani-King sold its first unit franchise in Oklahoma.
And the thing it sold
was not what anyone expected.
A normal franchise sells a brand,
a recipe, and a manual.
Jani-King sold something rarer: customers.
The regional office signed cleaning contracts, then handed
them to the franchisee as initial business.
Read that again, because it is the mechanism.
The franchisee did not start with
an empty book and a hope.
They started with paying customers on day one,
found and signed by the regional office.
That is why the model spread.
A cleaner who wanted their own business faced
the same wall McGuffin had faced: no time
to find work while doing the work.
Jani-King removed the wall.
The company's own history says it plainly.
Jani-King obtains the commercial cleaning accounts, and offers
the franchisee an initial customer base to service.
The customer is the product.
Here is what initial business means in practice.
On one Canadian plan, five thousand dollars of initial
business is the total dollar value of a
customer's monthly billing, handed to the new owner.
The franchisee still cleans.
They still hire, still train, still answer the
phone at midnight when a floor floods.
What they do not do is start from zero.
And the regional office does
not disappear after the handover.
It bills the customer, collects the money,
handles the paperwork, and sells the
franchisee more accounts as they grow.
That is the second half of the trick.
The franchisee gets customers.
The regional office keeps the relationship, the billing,
and the right to sell the next account.
Both sides need each other.
It worked because of a simple human fact
the founder had learned in nineteen sixty-nine.
A business owner cleans better than an
employee, because the owner keeps the profit.
Here is the second payoff.
The franchisee buys customers, not just a brand.
And the regional office that sold them those
customers takes a cut of every dollar those
customers pay, for as long as they stay.
That cut is where the empire's money lives.
Which brings us to the question every viewer asks
next: how much money are we actually talking about?
The disclosure document has the answer.
Every franchise in America must publish a disclosure document,
and Jani-King's tells you the price of admission.
A single-unit franchise costs roughly sixteen thousand
to fifty-seven thousand dollars to start.
That range depends on the plan and the
region — a bigger starting bundle of customers
costs more, a smaller one costs less.
The franchise fee itself runs from fourteen
thousand to thirty-five thousand dollars and up.
Now the other side of the ledger.
The disclosure document reports the average unit's gross
sales at about a hundred and eighteen thousand
dollars a year, from twenty twenty-four data.
Stop on that number, because it
is the one people misread.
A hundred and eighteen thousand dollars is gross sales.
It is what the customers pay, before anyone takes
a cut, buys supplies, or pays a cleaner.
And the cuts are real.
The royalty is ten percent of monthly gross revenue.
The accounting and sales fee is seven percent.
The advertising fee is one and a half percent.
Add them up, and about eighteen cents
of every dollar goes back in fees
before the owner sees a cent.

But the real story is not the money. It is a trick, and the trick is in chapter three. He never sold cleaning. He sold customers. And once you see the trick, you will see it in every franchise you have ever walked past. Jim Cavanaugh was a business student at the University of Oklahoma, and to pay his way he took the night shift at a Holiday Inn in Norman: night auditor, the man who balanced the books while the town slept. The night auditor's job was numbers, not mops. He checked guests in late, checked the ledger, and waited for morning. And every night, the same man mopped past his desk. That man was Don McGuffin, the hotel's night janitor. He cleaned the same floors Cavanaugh walked, and the two of them became friends in the small hours, when nobody else was awake to talk. McGuffin had a complaint, and it was not about the pay. He and his crew were so busy cleaning at night that he had no time left to look for new business during the day. Think about that problem. In nineteen sixty-nine, Cavanaugh borrowed three thousand dollars from a school friend and founded Jani-King. Three thousand dollars, a borrowed stake, and a borrowed idea. Three thousand dollars is not much. It would not buy a truck, a crew, or an office. What it bought was time: time to sell during the day without starving at night. metadata.author: Janitorial Empire
metadata.shortDescription:
How much should you charge to clean a 10,000 sq ft commercial building?

In this video, we break down a real commercial cleaning pricing example step by step — including labor hours, employee wages, labor burden, supplies, equipment, overhead, profit margin, and the final monthly selling price.

Using a 10,000 sq ft professional office cleaned 5 nights per week, you’ll see how to build your price from the actual cost of doing the work instead of simply guessing a price per square foot.

In this example, we cover:

✅ Estimating monthly labor hours
✅ Calculating your true labor cost
✅ Adding payroll burden
✅ Supplies and equipment costs
✅ Business overhead
✅ Markup vs. profit margin
✅ Calculating a 25% profit margin
✅ Building the final customer quote

Our example lands at approximately **$3,600 per month**.

The goal is simple: know your numbers before you submit your proposal.

If you're building or growing a commercial cleaning or janitorial business, subscribe to Janitorial Empire for practical strategies on pricing, finding clients, winning contracts, building teams, and growing a profitable cleaning company.

#CommercialCleaningBusiness #JanitorialBusiness #CleaningBusiness

segments.text: Surety bonds offer insurance agents a
unique opportunity to differentiate
their agency by providing an essential
business product that can lead to many
other insurance selling opportunities.
In this video, we explain why surety
bonds are a hidden gem for insurance
agents.
Most surety bonds are required by a
government agency and serve as a
prerequisite to obtaining a business
license or beginning work on a
construction contract. Obtaining a
surety bond is essential to all those
who need one. Including these in your
product offerings allows you to provide
an increased level of value to your new
and existing customers.
Many new businesses will need to
purchase a surety bond before commencing
operations. While this initial
transaction may be minuscule, agents
with the foresight to market bonds can
leverage access to these new businesses
to offer other core insurance lines like
general liability, commercial auto, etc.
Prospecting new businesses creates
long-term relationships that grow over
time as the insurance needs become
greater.
The underwriting for surety bonds
usually involves a review of the
business owner's credit and financial
statements.
Due to the personal nature of the
underwriting information, business
owners are unlikely to jump ship to
another agent after providing these
details.

videos.full_text: Surety bonds offer insurance agents a unique opportunity to differentiate their agency by providing an essential business product that can lead to many other insurance selling opportunities. In this video, we explain why surety bonds are a hidden gem for insurance agents. Most surety bonds are required by a government agency and serve as a prerequisite to obtaining a business license or beginning work on a construction contract. Obtaining a surety bond is essential to all those who need one. Including these in your product offerings allows you to provide an increased level of value to your new and existing customers. Many new businesses will need to purchase a surety bond before commencing operations. While this initial transaction may be minuscule, agents with the foresight to market bonds can leverage access to these new businesses to offer other core insurance lines like general liability, commercial auto, etc. Prospecting new businesses creates long-term relationships that grow over time as the insurance needs become greater. The underwriting for surety bonds usually involves a review of the business owner's credit and financial statements. Due to the personal nature of the underwriting information, business owners are unlikely to jump ship to another agent after providing these details.

metadata.title: Here’s what you need to know for your first post construction cleaning (I wish I would have known)
metadata.author: Nova Cleaners
metadata.shortDescription:
If this is your first post construction cleaning, or perhaps you want to tackle your own home renovation clean up. Here are things that will save you tons of time. 

#cleaningtips #postconstructioncleaning #postrenocleaning #smartcleaning #howtoclean #whatyouneedforyourjob #windowcleaning #dusting #sanddust

Find products here 

Shop vac https://amzn.to/4ay0MgI

Steamer https://amzn.to/3E33wq3

Push broom https://amzn.to/4g87CdK

High reach duster https://amzn.to/4g9dwLE

Grout brush https://amzn.to/3CgWu0m

segments.text: let's talk about post construction
cleanups I remember my very first job
was in fact a post construction cleaning
and to be honest I didn't know much
about it so I want to save you a lot of
trouble and some headaches by giving you
some pointers so you're prepared and
know what to do so the first thing is
obvious but you definitely need a good
quality shop back don't over complicate
it but make sure it has the proper
filters for the fine construction dust
that is very important now the next
thing whether you know it or not but you
are going to run into a lot of adhesive
that needs to be cleaned up so two
things that are going to come in really
handy one thing is gooone this product
works really well and the other thing is
a steam cleaner now that being said if
you don't have the budget yet to get a
steam cleaner make sure you have
something for adhesive cleanups the next
thing you need to think about is every
construction site has a messy painter so
if there's a really big job that needs
to be done as far as paint cleanup goes
a paint thinner will will definitely
come in handy another thing to keep in
mind is window cleaning so here are two
things you need for post construction
window cleanups one you need a good
quality scraper this is going to come in
really handy you might not know it yet
and the other thing is a brush for the
window sills so you can brush out at the
same time you're using a shop vac if you
don't have a bristle brush for the shop
vac and make sure you get everything
lifted up so you can suck all the
construction dust out of those window
sills don't show up to a post
construction cleanup without a broom and
a push broom you're going to need both
you'll thank me later everyone enjoys
nice light fixtures until they have to
dust it so make sure for the
construction cleanup you're ready to
have something that you can reach up
high for
dusting because this is definitely going
to be an important part of the post
construction cleaning make sure to have
a brush ready to go for tile and grout
cleaning this is another thing that
often gets overlooked but that fin
construction dust will definitely seep
into the grout lines and without this
it's going to be very tough to clean and
the other thing I mentioned before the
steam cleaner I know it might not be in
your budget yet but I can tell you right
now if I knew then what I know now I
never would have showed up to a
construction cleaning without a solid
steam cleaner just for example stainless
steel a lot of people make the mistake
of trying to clean it with a stainless
steel polisher that leaves a lot of
streaks and it doesn't look nice if you
use a steam cleaner with a microfiber
cloth you get really great results so
you don't have to go crazy but a good
quality steam cleaner will definitely
save you a ton of time another thing to
keep in mind are the hard-to-reach
places so definitely bring a step ladder
or a small ladder to help you reach all
those spots and of course soon you will
realize that cleaning construction dust
with a shop back is only half the battle
the embedded stuff that construction
workers walk over that is is the tough
stuff you can use a regular mob and a
cleaning solution and you'll be mobing
that over and over again so make sure to
do some homework and figure out what
cleaning chemical works best and what
size mop works best I would recommend a
commercial mop but if you're cleaning a
floor that can't be heavily saturated
that is not the right thing to do so
make sure to do your homework on the
place you're going to clean and remember
if all you got is a broom and some
microfiber cloths and a spray B model
don't let these pointers stop you the
best thing you can do is go out there
and start doing your first job so you
learn when I first started that's pretty
much all I had as well so you're going
to learn along the way these pointers
will just save you a ton of time if you
can afford to implement a few of these
things it'll definitely help but it
should never be a deal breaker go out
and get your jobs
